389/Lectures/Week-13.2---Cinematics.title: Week 13.2 — Cinematics
389/Lectures/Week-13.2---Cinematics.content:
Today’s agenda — Cinematics (techniques for creating cutscene cinematics in Unity), Portfolios (looking at portfolio pages from students and recent graduates), and the Salmond Reading discussion.
A workshop session: walk through Unity’s Timeline + Recorder for building cutscene cinematics, then look at example portfolio pages from recent students and graduates, then discuss Sylvester’s Engines of Experience chapter.










Interactive Lights and Cameras
Let’s open up Unity! Download and open the Timeline demo project.










Timeline — opening the window
Open the Timeline window and dock it somewhere convenient.

Window > Sequencing > Timeline

I like to dock the Timeline at the bottom of the editor window, along with the Project and Console windows. It’s useful to have a wide space to work with.










Timeline Asset
A timeline needs to be connected to both a GameObject on the Hierarchy and an asset in the project files.
Create an empty GameObject and call it Timeline. When you select it, the Timeline window will prompt you to create the Timeline asset. Save this asset somewhere appropriate in your project folder.










Lock Window View
Once you create your Timeline asset, you’ll want to lock your Timeline window to the Timeline GameObject. (Otherwise, it will try to show a new timeline whenever you select a different GameObject.)
Click the lock icon on the top right hand corner of the Timeline window.










Animation Track
An animation track can change the transform of a GameObject and interpolate between different transform values.
Drag any GameObject into the left side of the Timeline and select Animation Track. For example, you can create an animation track for a camera.
Click on the record button on the animation track to begin recording. Move the playhead to a time on the timeline and adjust the object’s transform to create a keyframe at that point. Move the playhead and create another keyframe, and the timeline will animate between them.










Activation Track
An activation track controls whether a GameObject is active or not.
Drag any GameObject into the left side of the Timeline and select Activation Track.
Right click on the timeline track and select Add Activation Clip. Adjust the starting and ending times of the clip on the timeline. During times when the clip is on the timeline, the GameObject will be active; whenever the clip is not on the timeline, the GameObject will be inactive.










Audio Track
An audio track can control what audio file plays from an Audio Source.
Drag an AudioSource into the left side of the Timeline and select Audio Track.
Right click on the timeline track and select Add From Audio Clip, or drag an audio asset directly into the timeline track. You can adjust the starting point of the track and see how the waveform will line up with other elements on your timeline. Remember that you can only play one audio file from an Audio Source at a time.










Unity Recorder
One more thing: Unity has a native recorder component that you can use to capture frames or video of your game. You have to download and install the Recorder package from the package manager, but it’s very easy to use.
Once you’ve installed the recorder, you can open the Recorder window from:

Window > General > Recorder > Recorder Window

When you start the recorder, it will automatically enter play mode and play your game. The recording will stop when you exit play mode. You can also set the recorder to automatically exit play mode if you end the recording from the Recorder window.
Add a new recorder. Make it a Movie Recorder. Check the settings. It will default to the same resolution as the Game window and save the video to a Recordings folder at the top level of your project.










Activity — Make a Cinematic
In small groups, use the Timeline and post processing effects to create a small cinematic cutscene. You should animate the camera and some lights.
You can use any assets you have access to, or grab some from www.kenney.nl/assets/category:3D.
Record your cinematic using the Unity Recorder and post it to the Discord.










Portfolios — approach as a design problem
A portfolio is interactive media! Approach your portfolio as a design problem, the same way that you would approach designing a game.
First step: What’s your experience goal? Think about what you want someone to understand about you when they look at your portfolio.
How can you present your work to create that understanding?










Portfolio examples
Michael Ford — Digital Design, Tabletop Design, Sound Design
Melody X Wang — www.melodyxwang.com/
Celine Tang — celinetang.com/games
Meny Menczel — www.menymenczel.com/
Thomas Lu — thomastianlu.com/










Flip the script
We don’t often talk about it in these terms, but flipping the script is a vital design skill. As a game designer, you have to think about what your game looks like to a brand new player. You’ve developed the skills to put yourself in that person’s shoes, even though you know a lot more about the game than they do.
Put yourself in the shoes of the person who’s looking at your portfolio. What do they want? What are they looking for? How much time are they going to spend looking at your website?
Use role-playing and playtesting to help get into the head of a reviewer!










Show your process
A potential employer is not just concerned with your product; in fact, they care even more about your process. Of course you want to put games that you’re proud of up on your portfolio, but it’s important that you explain what you contributed to the game and how you do your work.
Show your process. This will give readers who understand design confidence that you also have good practices. It also demystifies design for readers who don’t have a lot of experience with these processes. And it can help turn a lackluster product into a valuable selling point.










Discussion — Experience Engines
Thoughts on making players feel things.
Discussion prompts:

What did you think of this chapter?
Do you agree that detecting and understanding subtle emotions is a designer skill? Do we value it appropriately?
Did any of Sylvester’s emotional triggers stand out to you, as particularly resonant or unjustified? (Emotion through learning, character arcs, challenge, social interaction, acquisition, music, spectacle, beauty, environment, technology, primal threats, and sexual signals.) Is this list complete?
How does emotional variation relate to your current prototypes?











See You Next Time
No reading for next week!
Upload your third prototype to the Drive. We will playtest on Tuesday.

389/Lectures/Week-15.2---Final-Games,-In.content:
Playtesting the final project, with a tour of past Intermediate-level (489) games as scope reference.
The session opens with peer playtesting of the final projects, then walks through a curated set of 489 student games — each chosen to illustrate what an appropriately-scoped Intermediate semester project looks like. Closes with the final assignment specification and a winter-break sendoff.










Playtesting — Final Project
Peer feedback.










489 Projects — Picnic Pals! (2023)

Picnic Pals! (2023).
Picnic Pals! is a great example of a single, fairly simple puzzle / optimization mechanic with a game developed around variations on that theme. The art is simple but effective, and there’s enough variety to keep the game interesting for a handful of levels. This is scoped well enough that it has a smooth progression and feels fairly polished.










489 Projects — Absolution (2024)

Absolution (2024).
Absolution is a mostly linear visual novel with a unique presentation and thoughtful interjections of player choice. It keeps its scope down by containing its length and mechanics, but does a great job of using art, animation, and visual effects to create a compelling interactive piece. The art and writing do the work, with less demanded from engineering or balancing interactions.










489 Projects — Isabella (2023)

Isabella (2023).
Isabella is a contained experience that’s almost scoped appropriately for Intermediate. There’s just one primary mechanic, but it’s used in a few different ways over a small handful of levels. You can see some rough edges around the art — especially in the later levels — but overall it works. There are cutscenes, but they’re short and you can see where corners were cut to get them done.










489 Projects — Silly Masterpiece (2024)

Silly Masterpiece (2024).
Silly Masterpiece is an example of a game that can show off programming more than art. The mechanics are simple but require some tricky implementation, and the character controller is highly polished. Meanwhile, the character is crude, but uses tweening and particle effects to give it life.










489 Projects — The Lantern (2024)

The Lantern (2024).
The Lantern was a very ambitious project that did a good job of scaling back when the team realized they wouldn’t be able to create as much content as they’d planned. In the end, the clear aesthetic vision helped hold the whole thing together, but it would have probably benefited from more focus on fewer mechanics.










489 Projects — Slash Bash (2024)

Slash Bash (2024).
Slash Bash is a constrained but impressive fighting game that made good choices about where to focus development time. It has controller support, heavy post-processing, and a training mode, but importantly it doesn’t try to do networking. Modular content like multiple characters and levels makes it easier to control scope.










489 Projects — Mango Goes to Mewsic School (2023)

Mango Goes to Mewsic School (2023).
Mango Goes to Mewsic School is something to aspire to. It won the Diversity in Video Games Competition at the Congressional Black Caucus’ 2023 Legislative Conference. It’s considerably more expansive and polished than most Intermediate projects, but it marks something close to the upper limit of what can be accomplished in a semester. If you are imagining something more ambitious than this, you should probably scale back a bit.

Submissions are open now for video games, board games, mobile games, personal projects, class projects, game jams, VR, AR, installations, and more from calendar year 2025.

389/Lectures/Week-2.1---Keys-and-Doors.title: Week 2.1 — Keys and Doors
389/Lectures/Week-2.1---Keys-and-Doors.content:
The Keys, the Doors, and All Those Problems









Playtesting — The Other Shoe
Peer feedback session on The Other Shoe — Expectation and Payoff.
For each project, identify the initial expectation, what produced it, and how the payoff fulfilled, complicated, or overturned it.











Keys and Doors
Raph Koster’s A Theory of Fun posits that “fun” describes a certain kind of learning that humans have evolved to be good at and feel rewarded for engaging in.
Specifically, fun refers to a practice of pattern recognition. Being able to look at a situation and predict the outcome of a certain action or configuration of elements is a survival trait.
According to this framework, all games are fundamentally about teaching the player how to play the game.

Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design.







The Value of Uncertainty
Week 2.1 - The Value of Uncertainty









The Talos Principle — one key, many doors

The Talos Principle (2014).
What The Talos Principle teaches its player is a variation of keys and doors — albeit an unusual one, where the same key is able to open several different kinds of doors.
Through about 2:30, what is the game teaching the player? How? What does the player understand about the game at any particular moment? In this section, one kind of key opens three kinds of doors.
But key-and-door obstacles are an extremely common design feature in games of all kinds.










Literal keys, literal doors

Pokemon Red/Blue (1996).
The simpliest possible - card key to get through the door.

Doom (1993).

GoldenEye 007 (1997).
Being told.










Keys that aren’t keys, doors that aren’t doors
Key-and-door puzzles don’t always feature literal keys and doors. Many implementations of this design involve other kinds of obstacles that impede progress and can be bypassed by finding or activating another game object.
Sometimes this is as simple as finding a button or a switch, rather than a key. Sometimes it can be more sophisticated and interwoven with plot or mechanics.

Portal (2007).










Narrative-embedded keys — The Last of Us

The Last of Us (2013) — getting through a door with a powered lock. Find a generator to turn on the electricity to make the door open. Uses narrative setting.

The Last of Us (2013) — find a dumpster to push into a location to jump high enough.










When the key is an ability
Sometimes the “key” isn’t an object in the world at all — it’s a new capability the player has gained.

Link’s Awakening (1993/2019).
Player gains ability: quasi-grappling hook, pulls bridge across.

Ori and the Blind Forest (2015).
-Double jump.

Affordances of Movement
How it feels to traverse the world.
A character controller is a set of decisions about what the player can and can’t do — what speeds, what jumps, what stops, what slides. Those decisions are the player’s primary experience of the game.
Vehicles can provide narrative justification for putting interesting constraints on player movement. These constraints create affordances on both sides — the designer gets richer terrain, the player gets a clearer set of verbs.










Constrained Movement — Vehicles

Donkey Kong Bananza (2025) — a tertiary minecart mechanic.
Donkey Kong Bananza has a tertiary mechanic where you ride in a minecart. These minecart sections change the movement paradigm for the game, constraining movement along the rails. This effectively makes parts of the game 1D or 2D, allowing the player to engage with complex mechanics without splitting focus. It also lets the camera make cinematic moves and creates interesting minigame segments.

Cruis’n USA (1994).
Racing games and rail shooters both use the conventions of vehicular movement to put the player on a track, giving an opportunity for “play” within a constrained field of movement. This constraint affords fun gameplay for the player, but it also allows the designer to create an interesting environment for that gameplay — using their knowledge of how the player is going to be moving through it.

Star Fox 64 (1997).








Constraints Create Challenge

Here’s another parable: golf is a game with the goal of putting a ball in a hole. That would be pretty easy — and boring — if you could just pick up the ball and drop it in. The rules of the game require you to stand really far away and hit the ball with a stick.
The constraints create the challenge. The challenge creates the fun.
Of course, you don’t need vehicles to constrain a player’s movement. Designing a character controller is all about deciding how it feels to move — what the player can and can’t do. But vehicles can provide narrative justification for interesting constraints in a way a generic character controller can’t.










Controlled Perspective

Haunted Mansion (Florida, circa 2016).
Dark rides exploit the viewer’s constrained movement and perspective to control pacing, create surprises, and pull off visual tricks — the hollow mask illusion, infinity mirrors, Pepper’s ghost. These effects only work because the visitor can only look from a specific position.
Compare with the billboarded sprites in Cruis’n USA — they only need to look correct from one angle because the player’s perspective is constrained to the camera’s track.









What Is a Spline?
A spline is a mathematically defined curve. Behind the scenes it uses a series of control points and tangents to calculate the shape of the curve.
Splines are a type of vector graphic — graphics defined by math — as opposed to raster graphics, which are made of pixels. (For reference: Adobe Illustrator is a vector program; Photoshop is raster-based.) Unity generally uses raster graphics to render your game, though UI elements contain some vector elements. You can use vector graphics if you like, with a package like Freya Holmér’s Shapes.
Related to vector-defined shapes, 3D modeling software (including ProBuilder) offers parametric models — shapes like arches and stairs where you input numbers to modify the shape. You can ask ProBuilder to create curved stairs, then change the diameter of the curve or the number of steps. The result, though, isn’t a purely mathematical shape like a line or sphere; it’s a set of points defining a mesh. That’s (sort of) the 3D equivalent of rasterization.
There are simpler and more complicated ways to create these curves: Catmull-Rom, B-splines, and hermite splines. The most basic kind is a bézier curve, a type of hermite spline. You can learn more about the math involved if you’re interested — but luckily, you don’t have to.










The Unity Splines Package
Unity has a package for authoring and working with splines. There’s a one-minute introduction to installing the package, setting up a spline, and adding a GameObject that animates along it.

Unity’s first-party Splines package.
The package has other features too, such as generating a surface or spawning instances of a prefab along the spline.

Spawning prefabs along a spline — like this train game.
Unity didn’t have a first-party splines package for many years, so various Asset Store developers stepped in to fill the gap — and those packages offer features the Unity one doesn’t. The Curvy package, for example, is one of the oldest and most built-out: it supports different types of spline, whereas Unity offers only bézier curves (the simplest, but the least flexible).




Constraints In Other Ways
What can be fun about constraining the player’s control?
Let us study:

Thirty Flights of Loving
Plug & Play
The Pedestrian
I Am Bread

389/Lectures/Week-4.1---Quandaries.title: Week 4.1 — Quandaries
389/Lectures/Week-4.1---Quandaries.content:
Goals and Rewards
Why do we do the things we do? Let’s start with a confession about decision-making.
When your friend Bob goes on vacation, he looks for a touristy shop where he can buy a Christmas ornament and a sticker to put on his luggage. He could be spending that time experiencing the place he’s traveled to — but instead he’s drawn to collect a memento of the trip.

A Joshua Tree ornament — the kind of memento that pulls attention away from the experience itself.

And the matching luggage sticker. The reward of having collected can outweigh the reward of being there.

In addition, he spent 3 hours snapping the perfect selfie to post online.







Games run on the same impulse. Much of play is players pursuing goals and rewards — and a designer’s job is to understand what makes a reward worth chasing, and what it costs the player to chase it.










Decisions in Space
Games can provide opportunities for players to make decisions — including through their spatial design. What are some examples? What goes into making those decisions?

New Super Mario Bros. U (2012).










Paths — Known and Unknown
Sometimes a game offers multiple paths with known trade-offs. One path might be riskier but offer greater rewards; another might take more time but offer a greater chance of success.
Other times a game offers a choice between a known path and an unknown one. How do players make that decision? (Reference the chapter of Algorithms to Live By about exploration and exploitation).

Inscryption (2021) — a branching map of nodes, where each step is a choice between known and unknown rewards.

Death Stranding (2019) — route planning across terrain, weighing the safe path against the fast or rewarding one.










The Sunk Cost Fallacy
Human beings have natural biases that cause us to prefer non-optimal choices. One of these is the sunk cost fallacy — our tendency to want to continue along a path we’ve already invested in, even when it would be objectively better to abandon that investment and start fresh.
What are some examples of the sunk cost fallacy influencing people’s choices?

Super Mario Bros. (1985).










Understanding the Dilemma
There is a real challenge in simply understanding a dilemma. What kinds of choices do you encounter in games? How are they presented so that you understand what you’re choosing? How do you understand the stakes?

Super Mario World (1990).










Risk and Reward
When a game presents two (or more) paths of unequal challenge and outcome. In the Super Mario 64 level pictured here, these might be literal paths: both lead to the same place, but one is more dangerous — and filled with treasure.

Super Mario 64 (1996).










Builds
Something you choose at the beginning of the game that affects your experience throughout. In Mass Effect, you choose a class at the start that shapes your abilities and weapons for the rest of the game. In Hades, you choose a weapon that determines your attacks for that run. In Magic: The Gathering, you build a deck that determines which cards you have access to and how likely you are to draw them.

Hades (2020).










Progression
Sometimes the game presents choices as you play that shape your strategy and let you determine your play style. In Baldur’s Gate 3, you choose your class and class options every time you level up. In Hades, you choose whether to seek boons from a particular god, and which one. In Deus Ex, you level up through a tech tree that lets you focus on combat effectiveness or stealth.

Baldur’s Gate 3 (2023).










Emotional Weight
A game’s dramatic elements can make choices difficult — or even present a situation as a dilemma when there isn’t really a meaningful choice to make. Game narratives present choices all the time, with varying stakes. Games with units or parties can create dilemmas by putting characters in danger with trade-offs.
Consider which party member you let die in a role playing game.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (2025).










Prisoner’s Dilemma
Games can use social pressure and game theory to create difficult choices, especially when other players are involved. Dead Last is a tabletop game in which two players split a pot of loot: each can choose a small share or a large share, but if both choose a large share, neither gets anything — and the loot is distributed among the other players instead.

Zero Escape: Virtue’s Last Reward (2012).

389/Lectures/Week-5.1---Lost-Woods.content:
On This Page

Getting lost
Mazes
Lost Woods as a guided experience
Forests on film
Assignment
Reading — Analyzing Architecture

Getting Lost
Study: Lost Woods

The art of getting lost and finding your way











When was the last time you got lost?










Venice, Italy

Venice — Piazza San Marco from above.

Piazza San Marco in a period painting.

Venice from above — the island and the Grand Canal.
Visiting an old city before cell phones was an experience.










Mazes — Navigation and Traversal
Mazes
Navigation and Traversal
Video games have a long history of using mazes as obstacles or challenges. But simple mazes are rarely satisfying experiences for players.
Why not?
What makes a maze more satisfying?

Pac-Man (1980).

Breath of the Wild — a labyrinth seen from outside.

*Low-poly trees laid out in a regular grid.











Return to Zork (1993) — a first-person maze corridor.
Return to Zork is a 1993 CD-ROM adventure game that is held in extremely high regard as a product of its time, representing both the cutting edge of computer graphics and the design sensibilities of the leading (though waning) PC genre.
It contains more than one example of a first-person maze that presents a simple, brute-force obstacle to the player.












A maze with its route drawn in red.











A maze mapped out screen by screen.
This sort of maze was a popular aesthetic in the mid to late 20th century, akin to the try-and-die dungeon design of OSR D&D like the Tomb of Horrors.  (Here is 1990’s King’s Quest V.)











There was a huge secondary market for “strategy guides” and 1-900 tip lines that just compiled maps so that you wouldn’t have to painstakingly draw them out yourself. (Here is 1990’s King’s Quest V.)










Lost Woods — A Guided Experience
Lost Woods

Ocarina of Time (1998) — the Lost Woods.
Mazes-as-mapping-exercises have fallen out of favor in recent decades.
There’s not a lot of nuance to the frustration of not being able to find your way, and there’s not a lot of satisfaction to be had from rote memorization of a safe route.










Lost Woods

But there’s another way to think about maze spaces in games, and that’s as a guided experience.
Mazes can make players disoriented, but they can also be opportunities to make them feel clever and give them a sense of mastery over a dangerous or mysterious environment.










Lost Woods

Ocarina of Time (1998).
Lost Woods










Lost Woods
Guiding the Player
The Lost Woods in Ocarina of Time aren’t just a maze.
The game tells you what to pay attention to and your attention guides you through the space. You can brute force this puzzle. You can draw or follow a map. But you don’t have to, because the game gives you the tools you need to find your way.
You might feel lost, but the game gives you a path to follow.

Consider These Paths With The Reading Analyzing Architecture
Paths, focal points, sightlines, sound, and recurring objects can make a complex space readable. Landmarks promise a destination, but in a Lost Woods they should orient the player only as much as the experience needs.

What gives the player a stable reference point?
What makes them doubt that reference point?
What cue eventually lets them turn confusion into mastery?

How do paths, thresholds, framing, light, focus, walls, and pits organize the player’s experience of a space?





















Player Attention
Players notice movement, brightness, saturation, contrast, the center of frame, threats, and interactables. In a forest, those cues can offer a direction without becoming an explicit arrow.
The design question is not simply “How do I hide the route?” It is: What does the player learn to notice, and how does that attention help them find their way?




Unity Essentials for Lost Woods
Use Unity 6 URP. Revisit the parts of Unity that will give the forest atmosphere and readable direction: materials, directional and point lights, fog, audio sources, cameras, particles, and prefabs.
The relevant technical reference is Week 1.2’s Unity Essentials review. The Lost Woods Template includes the character controller and forest assets so that your effort can go into the player’s experience of the space.

389/Lectures/Week-8.1---Unreal-Tutorial.title: Week 8.1 — Unreal Tutorial
389/Lectures/Week-8.1---Unreal-Tutorial.content:
A tour of the Unreal Editor and Blueprints — orienting Unity-trained designers in a second engine.
This session is a hands-on orientation to Unreal Engine for the upcoming Unreal Tutorial project: navigating the editor (with constant reference to its Unity equivalents), an introduction to Blueprints visual scripting, and how to package a build to playtest in class.










Navigating the Unreal Editor
Unreal organizes a game much like Unity does, with different names:





























UnrealUnity equivalentProjectProjectLevelsScenesRegionsAsync ScenesActorsGameObjectsComponentsComponents
To create a new project, select the Games category and choose the template that best fits your project. Make sure Project Defaults are set to Blueprint and target the Desktop platform. Pick a quality preset (maximum or scalable, based on your hardware) and a template — First Person, Third Person, and so on.

The Unreal Project Browser — choose Games, then a template; set defaults to Blueprint and Desktop.
Viewport. A familiar window that renders a free perspective of the level. In Unreal, the viewport is both the editor view and the game view — this is where the game happens when you play in editor.

The Unreal Editor — viewport in the center, Outliner and Details on the right.
Navigating the viewport: right-click to look around, WASD or arrow keys to fly, scroll wheel to truck in and out, F to focus on a selected object.
Outliner. Analogous to Unity’s Hierarchy (though Unreal is much less robust in its hierarchical relationships). Here you’ll find all the actors in the level, visible and invisible — listed alphabetically, organizable into folders.
Search. Unreal is very focused on search as an organizing principle, with robust search tools you’ll use extensively.
Details. Equivalent to Unity’s Inspector — see the components of the selected actor and modify their public variables.
Toolbar. Prominently displays the most useful editor functions: saving, source control, and playing the level in editor.
Content Drawer. Equivalent to Unity’s Project window — all your game assets as organized in the file structure. (Search is useful here too.)

The Content Drawer — Unreal’s Project window.
In the top-right of the viewport are the familiar transform tools (translate, rotate, scale), snapping controls (toggle positional/rotational grid snapping and adjust grid size), and a view speed control (effective speed is the increment × the scalar).
Place Actors (Window → Place Actors) is a toolbox of common actors you can drag straight into the viewport.
One important difference from Unity: Unreal treats the player character specially. The player character is a special type of actor that doesn’t get placed in the editor. Instead, every level should have a PlayerStart actor as the spawn point. Don’t place a player character into the level, or Unreal will get confused.










Blueprints
Blueprints are node-based programming laid out visually like a flowchart. Nodes are connected by wires (or “noodles”). You can do a lot through Blueprint scripts on characters and objects: pick up and interact with items; trigger events, animations, and state changes; control platforms, elevators, and enemies; spawn and destroy objects. They’re very good for scripting actors for level and quest design, and they’re tightly integrated with the engine.
Create a new Blueprint Class from the Blueprints menu (or convert a selected static mesh into one). It opens in a new window: the Viewport tab is where you see the actor and add components; the Event Graph tab is where you author logic to give it behavior.

The Blueprint editor — Viewport tab for components, Event Graph for logic.
Variable types you’ll use as a beginner:













































TypeWhat it holdsBooltrue / falseIntegersigned 32-bit whole numberFloatdecimalStringtext that can be modifiedTextimmutable, localized (international) textVector3 floats — normally XYZ or RGBRotator3 floats — roll (X), pitch (Y), yaw (Z)Transform3D position, rotation, and scaleObjectany object (actor, light, mesh, sound, etc.)

The beginner Blueprint variable types.
The execution wire — the white noodle — dictates the sequence of execution through the Blueprint. Command nodes (which perform an action) and flow-control nodes must be connected to it to run. Some query nodes (which return values) don’t connect to it; their values are pulled in when a connected node executes.
Event nodes trigger execution:

BeginPlay happens once, when the actor is instantiated.
Tick happens every frame the actor exists.
ActorBeginOverlap happens whenever the actor overlaps a collision volume.


The core event nodes — BeginPlay, Tick, and ActorBeginOverlap.
Flow control nodes can split the execution wire, but these are never parallel threads — execution always follows one wire at a time, in strict sequence.
Debugging. The Print String node prints a string to the top-left of the play screen — useful for debugging. You can also set breakpoints to pause execution at a node and inspect program state, or simply watch the execution flow on the Blueprint while the game runs (a second screen helps).

Print String, fired by an overlap trigger — a quick debug readout.
Variables can be open (public) or closed (private). Closed variables are good for internal state; open variables communicate info between Blueprints.
Triggering on proximity. Give the Blueprint actor a Collision component and use casting to detect the player. (In the Third Person template, the player actor is of type ThirdPersonCharacter.)
Animating an actor. Use a Timeline to drive a transformation (like a change in position). A Timeline defines an animation/tween curve for some value; its Update wire executes rapidly for the length of the Timeline, smoothly translating the object over time.

A Timeline drives smooth, curve-based animation from Blueprints.










Build & Export
You can build an executable with default settings by clicking the Platforms button on the toolbar, selecting your platform, and packaging the project.

Package a build from the Platforms menu on the toolbar.
Always make a build to playtest in class — playtesting on SCA’s virtual workstations doesn’t work very well. Give yourself time: if you use any advanced features, a build can take a while to complete.

389/Lectures/Week-8.2---Subtext-and-Them.title: Week 8.2 — Subtext and Theme
389/Lectures/Week-8.2---Subtext-and-Them.content:
How games carry meaning through metaphor — from Alice in Wonderland to surrealism to the controlling metaphor of Papo y Yo.
This session traces the arc of experience called subtext and theme: how games ask players to make sense of the seemingly nonsensical, how metaphor scales from a single phrase to an entire work, and how surrealism turns the unconscious into a puzzle to be solved. It also covers CSG brushes for grayboxing in Unreal, and closes with a close-reading discussion of Papo y Yo.










Alice in Wonderland — the precursor
Alice in Wonderland is an essential precursor to video games. We know this because when designers insert a reference to it in their game, they do so to signal the player to take on a mindset: moving the incomprehensible to the understood so the player can proceed — just like Alice did.

Alice in Wonderland — the high table, the bottle labeled “Drink me,” the key, the door too small to fit through.
Take a look at the scene: at first it appears to be nonsense. But on closer inspection, sense-making is possible — through trial and error, these elements connect and logic emerges. Many video game situations work this way: the player enters a room and, in order to proceed, must make sense of the space as a puzzle before they can solve it.
References to Alice are common (see Why Videogames Love Alice in Wonderland by Matt Margini). As Margini notes, Carroll asks the reader to puzzle through linguistic inversions, looking not necessarily for meaning but for logical — or at least ludic — consistency. In what we’ll loosely call surrealist games, the player essentially takes on Alice’s role: transforming the situation from the illogic of the unconscious mind to a conscious logic.

Breath of the Wild (2016) — spaces that ask to be read, independent of surrealism.










Metaphor
Subtext is a device used in every form of art — there’s a theme to be found or unlocked when we do the work. And we can read subtext after we decipher metaphor.
From “What is Metaphor?” by Tim Jensen (Oregon State University): a metaphor is a comparison between two otherwise-unrelated things, where the qualities of one are figuratively carried over to another. When I say “Dude, I’m drowning in work,” I’m using the urgency and helplessness of drowning to convey something about my workload. Metaphors let us see things from different angles and in a new light — both of which are, themselves, metaphors.
Three scales of metaphor:

Short — so brief it might be simpler than a metaphor. “The house is a house” prepares us to read one thing as another. (Are the gears in Papo y Yo a metaphor? The lemons are simpler than the frogs — you can describe the lemons’ role in one sentence; the frogs take two.)
Extended — goes on for several sentences. We take multiple steps to get there. Does that make the metaphor richer?
Controlling — extended across an entire piece. We’ll discuss Papo y Yo’s controlling metaphor.


Papo y Yo (2012).
Metaphors are fundamental to creative expression — they convey complex emotions and ideas in novel, engaging ways, and they make information more memorable by creating mental associations between concepts. When you’re given a puzzle made of object-metaphors, it’s not for the sake of simplification: the goal is to arrive at meaning and make that comprehension your own. Coupled with problems to solve, metaphors invite you to draw parallels between a known situation and an unknown one, gaining insight and finding solutions to unfamiliar challenges.

Opus Magnum (2017) — a puzzle as metaphor.










Surreal — and Surrealism
When you’re given a puzzle as metaphor, we can understand it as surreal — but we should be careful using the term freely. “Surreal” is overused in everyday speech. Surrealism was a European art movement from about 100 years ago. It featured illogic to draw attention to the unconscious mind; interpreting and configuring the work into a logical meaning is the role of the viewer.

Les Mystères du Château de Dé (1929).
Perhaps more than any other genre, surrealism features surprise (which sounds useful for game designers). Surprises come small and extended; non-sequiturs can be made meaningful if you make the effort. The reader is not passive.
Concurrent with surrealism in the early 20th century — or perhaps an essential influence — psychoanalysis articulated that the mind was a puzzle waiting to be interpreted and solved. Whether or not you believe its concepts, the premise is that events in childhood shaped how we relate to life today, and moving memories, thoughts, and feelings from the unconscious to the conscious mind brings insight. When that relationship is manifested as a metaphorical puzzle, it’s thrilling to play.
There are more than a few surreal video games: Superliminal (2019), Maquette (2021), Baba Is You (2019), That Dragon, Cancer (2016), Everything (2017), Back to Bed (2014), Antichamber (2013), and Inside (2016) among them.

Superliminal (2019).

Inside (2016) — how do we reconcile the unconscious and conscious mind through play?
Sometimes the character is only a vehicle — very different from the narrative arc we studied recently. In Papo y Yo, the author’s daydream is on display: he’s literally working out his childhood traumas and inviting us to shape the experience from an unconscious representation into our conscious understanding.










CSG Brushes
Unreal has a system for quickly implementing Constructive Solid Geometry that lets you easily build temporary layouts, furniture, or even simple structures for prototyping.

CSG brushes in the Place Actors panel, under Geometry.
CSG (also known as Binary Space Partition) is a technique for roughing out — blocking, or grayboxing — the static contents of a level before art is added. Typically it’s not used for final models (those get replaced by model meshes), though it might be used for collision geometry in production. Find the CSG brushes in the Place Actors tab under the Geometry section, and drag them into your viewport or World Outliner.
CSG brushes can be set as additive or subtractive — subtractive elements carve holes or pockets out of normal elements. Set this in the Details pane for the brush.

Additive vs. subtractive brushes — subtractive carves holes.
You can also edit CSG brushes directly: manipulating faces, edges, or vertices; extruding faces; and drawing new vertex geometry. Access Brush Editing mode through the Modes drop-down in the toolbar.










Discussion — Papo y Yo

Papo y Yo (2012) — a close reading.
Work through these questions as a close reading of the game’s subtext:

What is Papo y Yo’s controlling metaphor?
What does Alejandra represent? What does Lula represent?
What is the subtext behind the environment design?
Many puzzles involve Quico manipulating the walls and buildings of the favela. What’s the subtext there?
What is the function of the slow-motion scenes?
After Lula is broken, Alejandra tells Quico there’s a way to cure Monster — his motivation for the second part of the game. What’s the meaning of this?
Did losing power (Lula) and backtracking have value?
What is represented by Quico taking on the same body paint Alejandra has?
We return to the starting location twice over the course of the game. What’s the significance?
What is the subtext of the game’s ending?

Reading — The Level Design Book
The Level Design Book by Robert Yang, Chapter 5: Blockout — book.leveldesignbook.com/process/blockout. Read by next Thursday; we’ll discuss in class.
We return to Yang’s book, this time for a chapter on blocking out levels. Blockout is an important part of pre-production and is ubiquitous in games with navigable 3D spaces. This chapter also activates concepts that will matter when we discuss divergent prototyping later in the semester.

389/Lectures/Week-9.2---Mechanics-and-Em.title: Week 9.2 — Mechanics and Emotion
389/Lectures/Week-9.2---Mechanics-and-Em.content:
The arc of experience where mechanics generate meaning — the self-conscious emotions games are uniquely able to evoke.
This session is about how mechanics elicit emotion, especially the self-conscious emotions — guilt, pride, fiero, naches, embarrassment, coliberation — that depend on the player reflecting on their own actions. It closes with the Values at Play brainstorming tool, a Blockout discussion, and the reading on the Game Design Macro.










Mechanics and Emotion
Mechanics define how the player relates to the player character and the world. Changing them causes the player to reevaluate their experience; mechanics that reflect the character’s experience draw the player into the character’s story. Has a game ever made you feel complicit?

Shadow of the Colossus (2005) — mechanics that make you feel the weight of your actions.










Guilt
Guilt is a self-conscious emotion — it involves reflection on oneself. Games are uniquely capable of eliciting it, because they take your own actions into account. Guilt is the feeling of deserving blame: when you do something you know is wrong, you’re conscious that you deserve blame for the outcome.
Of course, “something you know is wrong” is context-dependent — and games can use that. The Millennial Fair sequence of Chrono Trigger (1995) presents itself as a typical RPG and expects you to behave like you’re playing one. But it’s been recording your behavior differently than usual, and later uses your antisocial actions as evidence against your character in a trial.

Chrono Trigger (1995) — the Millennial Fair turns your behavior into evidence.
Teddy Diefenbach made this the subject of his 2012 MFA thesis, The Moonlighters, calling the technique narrative listening — where the game pays attention and responds to player actions at a level often dismissed as noise in the system.
Games don’t have to resort to trickery, though. Plenty present difficult choices and then play out the consequences.

This War of Mine (2014).

Papers, Please (2013) — pressuring players into choices they’ll feel guilt or pride about.
The flip side of guilt is pride — feeling righteous for an action you believe was right despite danger, difficulty, or consequence. Games can be designed to pressure players toward choices they’ll feel guilty or proud of; either way, the game leans on the player’s ability to feel self-consciously.

BioShock (2007) — moral dilemmas working the guilt/pride range.










Fiero
Fiero is the sense of satisfaction derived from one’s achievements — the self-conscious emotion most commonly accessed by games. Most games are built around giving the player a sense of accomplishment on completing a level or finishing the game.

Elden Ring (2022) — soulslike difficulty engineered for fiero.
Soulslike games do this very deliberately: completing a challenge typically requires mastery — learning a boss’s patterns, patience, the right gear and skills, “gitting gud” — so it often takes many attempts. Players are drawn to the satisfaction of overcoming.
But difficulty isn’t the only path. The 2008 meme game You Have to Burn the Rope deliberately rejects difficulty, making gameplay as easy as possible — and yet the player still feels satisfaction at the end. That feeling doesn’t come from overcoming a challenge; it comes from having correctly followed the instructions and received praise for doing so.

You Have to Burn the Rope (2008) — fiero without difficulty.
Players can feel similar satisfaction for subverting instructions — wandering off a quest, killing an NPC, exploiting a glitch. The satisfaction is greater when the game acknowledges what happened.

The Stanley Parable (2011) — satisfaction in defying the game’s instructions.










Naches
Naches is a Yiddish word for the pride a parent or mentor takes in the accomplishments of their child or student. It’s a niche emotion, but certain genres align with it specifically, using virtual agents the player can mentor or influence.

Black & White (2001) — training a creature you take naches in.
It’s an old idea — the inspiration behind the 1996 Tamagotchi craze and 2005’s Nintendogs, and the creative pillar of “artificial life” games like 1996’s Creatures (agents that learn via neural networks and evolve via genetic algorithms). Black & White (2001) gave the player indirect control via a giant avatar creature they train as a pet.










Embarrassment
Embarrassment is the feeling that your shortcomings are being judged by others. It’s fundamentally social — based on how you relate to others and how your actions are perceived.

Lollipop Chainsaw (2012) — publicly shaming the player for an action.
In Lollipop Chainsaw (2012), players who positioned the camera to look up the protagonist’s skirt earned a publicly-visible achievement, “I Swear! I Did It By Mistake!” The game — crude and tongue-in-cheek — makes a joke of exposing the player.
Social games, especially party games, can use embarrassment as motivation, punishment, and a method for bonding. Embarrassment stems from feeling vulnerable, and having your vulnerability accepted by your social circle can be affirming.










Coliberation
Coliberation is Bernie DeKoven’s word for the feeling of participating in something larger than oneself — evoked by religious practice, cooperating with a team, or a “well-played game.” Even two opponents facing each other competitively are also collaborators, working together to play a game well according to agreed-upon rules.
Professional athletes compete fiercely — violently, in American football — yet outside the game can feel respect, friendship, and admiration for opponents. The NFL practice of jersey trading is a great example: players bonded by mutual participation. Wins and losses come and go, but the sport is more important than any single contest.










Agency
Agency (self-efficacy) is the feeling that you have the capability to effect change — that what you do matters. In many ways it’s an overriding emotion: guilt, pride, fiero, and the rest all rest on the belief that your actions matter. If you don’t feel you have agency, you won’t feel complicit in any outcome.
The most important thing to recognize as a designer is that agency is subjective. You can design a game whose outcome changes radically based on player actions, but if the player doesn’t realize they’ve influenced it, they feel no agency. To make the player feel agency, the game must send clear signals about what choices they’re making and how those choices affect the game’s state.
Two related traps in how a system appears:

The ELIZA Effect — when the player’s experience of a system suggests complexity that isn’t actually there. It’s a trick: a way to make the player feel more is going on than really is. Useful, but dangerous — if the player interacts enough to figure out how it really works, they’ll feel cheated.
The Tale-Spin Effect — when the player’s experience obscures the complex mechanisms creating it. (Noah Wardrip-Fruin’s example: Tale-Spin’s rich internal simulation of characters’ goals and plans never surfaces in its output — the hidden action can’t be deduced from what’s shown.)


ELIZA (1967) — the original effect named after it.
Multiple endings are one way games tell you your choices matter; recognizing that a game has them is one way a player feels agency. Players often read variable endings as good/bad, where bad endings are a failure state.

Persona 5 — endings that signal your choices mattered.
In 2012, Mass Effect 3 earned scorn for boiling all of players’ investment down to a choice between three similar endings — leaving many feeling their actions hadn’t mattered after all. I like to contrast this with Beyond: Two Souls (2013), which offers a final choice in a way reminiscent of Mass Effect 3 — but the choice isn’t primarily about what happens. The events play out more or less the same way; what changes is how the player character feels about them.

Beyond: Two Souls (2013) — a final choice about feeling, not outcome.










Values at Play
Grow-a-game cards are a brainstorming tool to help designers think critically about the themes and messages their games communicate, and to imagine games that explore less common themes. The tool has four decks; we’ll focus on two:

Grow-a-game cards — verbs and values for design brainstorming.

Verbs are game mechanics — what the player can do to act within the system: run, jump, shoot, buy, give…
Values are dynamic elements — what behaviors the game rewards: violence, teamwork, speed, planning, patience…

The exercise. Pick a verb and a value. What might a game look like that used the verb as a core mechanic and expressed the value? Form a small group; I’ll give each group a couple of verbs and values. Explore the potential meanings of each, think about how they might interrelate, and come up with a potential game or activity based on that relationship.
Discussion — Blockout
Working from the Yang reading:

What did you think of this chapter?
How do “blockouts support experimentation”?
Yang says using 3D art tools (Blender, Maya, SketchUp) for blockouts is controversial. Where do you fall?
Section 4 is titled “Diverge and iterate.” Divergence is an important concept that will come up again — what does it mean?

Reading — The Game Design Macro
Playful Production Process by Richard Lemarchand, Chapter 17: The Game Design Macro. Read by next Thursday. This is the textbook that underpins CTIN 489; we’ll look at just one chapter, describing the Game Design Macro — a piece of design documentation you’ll begin using in just about all your classes. (In the Readings folder on our Drive.)
See You Next Time
Upload the final build of your Unreal Interaction Project to the Drive — we’ll playtest on Tuesday.

389/Lectures/Week-x.y---The-Value-of-Unc.title: Week x.y — The Value of Uncertainty
389/Lectures/Week-x.y---The-Value-of-Unc.content:
Sources
The Value of Uncertainty
Four Authors – philosophers and psychologist
aeon.co/essays/use-uncertainty-to-leverage-the-power-of-your-predictive-brain










keywords
Certainty, uncertainty, volatility, surprise, explore, information, solution, control










Three Stages
3 Stages


Expected Uncertainty


Unexpected Uncertainty


Volatility












Concepts
First, let’s focus on some concepts.










Mental Model


What a person believes or thinks they know about a system


A person’s expectations of an external reality, a simplified version


Constructed from their past experiences













A retail site interrupts the visit with an email-capture pop-up.

A newsletter page and its navigation rail.
Because of the pop up, clicking the back button takes them back to google, the actual first page.










Predictive Processing
Human brains are designed to minimize their own average surprise (prediction error) during
real-life exchanges with the world.










Predictive Processing: Peter’s Preemptive Summary
When we find ourselves at a prediction level at “medium” as opposed to “excellent” or “terrible”, we respond by seeking more information for our model – compelling us to be open to learning and exploring.
This can be fun. (Careful with that word, “fun”).


                  
                  Instructor shares 
                  
                

This is Peter’s interpretation and take. Including coupling learning with fun.












We probe the world in ways that aim to reveal just where the key uncertainties lie, so that by future actions they can resolve them and move on.
We seek new information and engage in complex rituals such as art…whose role is to safely reveal and stress-test our own deepest assumptions.










epistemic (knowledge-seeking)
pragmatic (puzzle-solving)










1. Expected Uncertainty
Expected uncertainty is experienced whenever we know the weak spots in our information, and we can take action accordingly (i.e. control).
We are equipped to ‘think things through’ in advance of acting because we have a workable mental model.










An example: registration
You want to enroll in a popular class that has 2 sections, but maybe 3.


The 8am (Bad) — T/Th. Undesirable time. Fills last, but it does fill.


The Monday night (Ok) — 6–9pm, one three-hour block. This is adequate.


The rumored Wednesday noon (Great) — drops between your two other classes. No extra trip to campus. Ideal.












The night before
You don’t know how fast the Monday (the OK one) night fills.
But you know the 8am (Bad) goes last. You know roughly how last year went. You wonder if the noon section (Great) is only a rumor.
You don’t know what will happen, but you know exactly where your ignorance is.










The plan is clean
Running “if I take the Monday night (OK), I still have a seat, and I can watch for noon (Great)” in your head, before touching the portal.
→ Thinking is an action. It harvests information from the model you already have.
And the plan is correct. Switching is free and easy, so grabbing a fallback costs you nothing. You end up with a seat either way, and the noon section stays in reach.










Precision
“We were told a third might open” — by whom?
A department admin’s email and a group-chat rumor are the same information at different confidence.
The confidence decides how much of the plan you build around it.










2. Unexpected Uncertainty
Unexpected uncertainty typically occurs when the environment (the rule structure) changes without our being in a position to predict that change.
This might be my cue to move into exploratory mode.
Predictive brains expect control and, if it fails, they drive learning.
We know there is a pattern. We just have to discover it.










The rule changes
You take the Monday night. And it fills.
Then the registrar posts a new drop/add rule — you have to drop a class before you can add another. There is not longer a ‘swapping’ option.
You know from past experience that dropping takes the system 5 to 30 minutes to complete.
Your plan wasn’t wrong. It was made under different rules.










Now it’s a dilemma
Explore vs. exploit. There was no tradeoff yesterday, because enrolling was free. This new delay in changing sections - a period of minutes in which you are enrolled in nothing - manufactures one.










What you do next
Email the advisor. Ask people who registered yesterday whether the lock hit them. Check whether it applies to waitlist auto-enrolls.
That’s the learning rate going up. You attempt discovery.
The registrar has rules. They’re just not published.










3. Volatility
Volatility is subtly different: it names a situation in which the frequency of changes in the rules or situation are themselves rapidly changing.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.










Registration, continued
Wednesday, the noon (Great) section is added. Just before you drop your OK section, the Great section is pulled. Phew.
Thursday it’s back with a cap of 10 students.
Friday there’s a rumor of another one.










You can’t learn a rate
There’s no strategy to form, because the thing you’d form it about won’t hold still.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.
You either freeze — stay in the Monday night (Ok), stop checking, let the noon section go —
or refresh the portal every ten minutes for four days and learn nothing.
That’s the tell: your choices stopped paying. What’s left is only how you cope with that.










Volatility
With unexpected uncertainty (#2), our strategies can work – in our mode of learning and openness.
But with volatility, our strategies are suspect. People and animals find this situation extremely uncomfortable.
Pony Island does volatility?!?  You tell me.








We recognize that our ability to discover is weak, therefore we have no control.










Marvel Snap
The same three stages, in a game










Marvel Snap — Expected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — the collection screen.
The Player,
“I don’t know exactly what is going to happen. But I am quite oriented.”










Marvel Snap — Unexpected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — building a deck.

*Marvel Snap
A new ability - a card whose On Reveal ability changes the location itself.*










Marvel Snap — Volatility
Our cards are taken away
and we are forced into
a “Redemption Round”


                  
                  Instructor notes 
                  
                

I made this up. I don’t know if I’m playing AI, if this round will win my cards back or if there’s no connection.
There’s no example in Marvel Snap because volatility is bad, so you’re not going to see it in a game like this.












Art
Art has expected uncertainty (#1),
and unexpected uncertainty (#2).
Our predictive models are encountered as objects →
we understand our own expectations.










This reveal can be a way of materializing and confronting our own high-level assumptions, about self, world and other, but doing so in a framework that steps back from daily concerns.











Certain and uncertain, against pretend (practice) and real.

Course Description
This course teaches fundamental skills of digital game development alongside the basic principles of level design. Over the semester, students will learn concepts related to the implementation and presentation of digital games using computer graphics, then demonstrate that learning through practical projects focused on specific game-development techniques.
Through these projects, students will practice level-design preproduction, layout, blockout, and production.
The course also covers professional communication for game designers, including techniques that support collaboration and conflict resolution.

Your grade in this course is based on conscientiousness: attending class and having work ready when it is scheduled for playtest.
Attendance and Punctuality
You receive one forgiven absence over the semester. Beginning with the second absence, each additional absence lowers the final course grade by 3 points. For example, a final grade of 100 becomes 97.
Four late arrivals, accumulated across the semester, count as one absence. That absence is included in the same forgiveness and subsequent deductions.
If Peter is ever late to class, attendance will not be taken that day. In addition, every student receives one additional forgiven absence to use later in the semester.
Playtest Builds
You receive one forgiven playtest without a working build over the semester. After that, each scheduled playtest for which you do not provide a working build ready for in-class play lowers the final course grade by 5 points.
Your grade begins at 100. Attendance and playtest-build deductions accumulate: for example, a second absence lowers a 100 to 97, and a second playtest without a working build lowers a 100 to 95. A final grade of 90–100 is an A; 80–89.9 is a B; and so on.

534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-1.title: Project 1 — The Investigator
534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-1.content:
Situated Player Role Reading: The Investigator — World as Evidence
Learning Goals: Color theory and lighting; interactive storytelling; arc of experience; game engine literacy; camera principles; materials and textures; sound design; ideation, brainstorming, and prototyping; self-direction; critique.
Team Size:  Solo.  A pair can request to work together by messaging Peter.  How will pairing up aid in your learning?
Deliverable: a built version of your Unity project.
Deadline policy: Submit by the scheduled class time. A project submitted within 24 hours after that time lowers the final course grade by 5 points. A project submitted more than 24 hours late, or never submitted, lowers the final course grade by 10 points.
Prompt: Create an Investigator project: a narrative space utilizing the principles of scripted spaces and environmental storytelling studied in class. The player should construct the story by investigating the world as evidence — reading, listening, seeing, finding, or collecting rather than receiving the story through exposition.
Ask yourself:

How is discovery at the heart of the experience?
*What does The Investigator do? Reads, listens, sees, finds, collects?
How do we distinguish the characters? Do we care?
What is the location? Is it interesting?
How are you designing for uncertainty? What is your model for how the player — at any given moment — knows just enough information to be curious and engaged?

Constraint: the entire project can have no more than 60 read-by-player words (not counting character names, menus, signs, UI, etc. — basically, no big blocks of text explaining the past or present of the world).
Turn in Folder: Project Turnin
Playtest: Guide

534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-2.title: Project 2 — The Traveler
534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-2.content:
Situated Player Role Reading: The Traveler — World as Presence
Learning Goals: Color theory and lighting; interactive storytelling; arc of experience; game engine literacy; camera principles; materials and textures; sound design; ideation, brainstorming, and prototyping; self-direction; critique.
Team Size: Solo or pair.
Like The Investigator project, this project also centers on the player’s experience of discovery.
Design a level featuring a multicursal maze (a maze with multiple paths) in which the player goes through 3 stages of experience, in order:

Feeling lost (with a sense of wonder)
Recognizing a pattern they suspect — maybe — will help them find their way (with a sense of excitement)
Finding their way, whether or not they understand how they did so (you decide which you want)

By the end, the player has an interpretation of what that experience was about — a personal interpretation. What did the sequence reveal to them? Pick only one to express:

A theme
A dilemma
A conviction
A question
Or a personal insight (for the player)

Consider the class’s discussions of modernism, particularly the role of interpretation as central to the experience — as opposed to a solution/configuration/win/lose mindset.
Primarily, The Traveler finds a path and bears witness to unfolding events.
What else might The Traveler do? Chooses, listens, backtracks, opens?
For the player, is this assignment, ultimately, about losing power, or realizing they never had it?
Furthermore, put time into lighting the world so that it reflects the mood of your game. Make it happen with lighting, sound, and use of camera mechanics (such as depth of field, focal length, aperture, angle, post-processing). Put all three of these audiovisual elements to use.

534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-3.title: Project 3 — The Dreamer
534/Assignments/534-Due-Project-3.content:
Situated Player Role Reading: The Dreamer — World as Enigma
Learning Goals: Color theory and lighting; interactive storytelling; arc of experience; game engine literacy; camera principles; materials and textures; sound design; ideation, brainstorming, and prototyping; self-direction; critique.
Create a short series of rooms — or equivalent — that the player must puzzle-solve to proceed from one space to the next. These spaces are surreal — they provide images and mechanics that are initially inexplicable, and presumably metaphorical. The player plays; they interpret the world, both as a puzzle and a playground of dreamlike metaphors.
Use Alice from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland as a model. Your player goes through the same internal stages she does:

Legibility — What are these objects? What do they do?
Opportunity — What are potential solutions? What can I imagine?
Performance — Can I execute that solution?

What does The Dreamer do? Configures, opens, interprets?
For any team still learning to code: consider the three stages above from the player’s point of view. Such teams are welcome to “dungeon master” outcomes with cheat keys, like the person who runs an escape room does — Peter will explain this in class.
Provide team names and a link to a Windows zipped downloadable by the scheduled class time. A project submitted within 24 hours after that time lowers the final course grade by 5 points. A project submitted more than 24 hours late, or never submitted, lowers the final course grade by 10 points.

534/In-Class/534-In-Class-Week-1.1-The-C.title: Week 1.1 — The Creativity Choice
534/In-Class/534-In-Class-Week-1.1-The-C.content:
Although we know that when people feel happy, they are generally more original and flexible in their thinking, researchers have also found that the benefit of these moods does not go far. It turns out that if people work on generating ideas for longer than four minutes, whether they are happy or not makes no difference: their creative ideas become similar in both their quality and the quantity, regardless of mood. Creativity that results in performances or products that make our lives better or easier does not happen in a few minutes. It takes anywhere from hours to days, sometimes many of them, for an artist to create a painting or a musician to write a song; months for designers and engineers to create a new mobile app; and years to develop a movie or an innovative new consumer product.
Pringle, Dr. Zorana Ivcevic. The Creativity Choice: The Science of Making Decisions to Turn Ideas into Action (pp. 3-4).
How could we describe creative individuals? After decades of study, we know that the central trait of those who are creative—artists and scientists, entrepreneurs, and innovative organizational leaders—is openness to experience. Being open to experiences means being curious, valuing aesthetic experiences, enjoying hearing about new ideas, having a vivid imagination, relishing thinking about things, and striving to carry conversations to a higher level. Open people are passionate about their interests, prefer variety to routine, are not attached to conventional ways of doing things, and embrace change.
Pringle, Dr. Zorana Ivcevic. The Creativity Choice: The Science of Making Decisions to Turn Ideas into Action (p. 4).
Interviews with eminent creators, from business leaders to prominent artists to Nobel Prize–winning scientists, point to another key feature of creative individuals’ personalities. They embody contradictions. Creative individuals hold traits that usually do not go together. They have great energy, especially when their work asks for it, but also often have periods of inactivity. They are playful but also disciplined and responsible. They have immense powers of imagination, yet are rooted in reality. They are passionate about their work, but they retain the ability to step back and look at it with detachment, which allows them to critically examine and further develop it. They have a capacity for both extraversion and introversion; they are able to engage with a broad range of people yet are also attracted to solitude and quiet. They recognize the creativity of their accomplishments and are proud of them. However, they do not tend to focus on their past achievements. The focus on their next idea or project keeps them humble. But again, although
Pringle, Dr. Zorana Ivcevic. The Creativity Choice: The Science of Making Decisions to Turn Ideas into Action (p. 5).
In my continued pursuit of answers to this question, I learned something especially heartening: the science of creativity is clear that rather than being an innate gift of the lucky few, we can learn to be more creative at any point in life, and creativity can be nurtured by others around us—
Pringle, Dr. Zorana Ivcevic. The Creativity Choice: The Science of Making Decisions to Turn Ideas into Action (p. 5).
