534/Lectures/Week-1---Narrative-Roles.title: Week 1 - Narrative Roles
534/Lectures/Week-1---Narrative-Roles.content:
Summary: Video games use image, sound, and text to communicate. This session sets up the cinematic vocabulary we will use all semester, then introduces four narrative roles — The Investigator, The Traveler, The Entrant, and The Dreamer — that organize your first three projects.










Course Overview



A Note on Terms
First!
This presentation refers to the creator as the “designer” or “filmmaker” and so on.
The audience and players will be referred to as “us” and “we”. And “our”.










Cinematic Language
Video games use image, sound, and text to communicate
This class will prioritize analyzing cinematic language.
We will study and practice every week.











Deep versus shallow focus on the same subject.
For example
Depth of field shapes our attention and our take on subjectivity.











The color wheel.
So does the use of color.











The Favourite (2018) - an extreme wide-angle lens distorts the room and the power in it.
Game engine cameras mimic the terms and features of physical ones, and cinematography broadly.
(Focal length, f-stops, lens filters, focus, light types, and so on).










So that (for example)
Creators can practice “show don’t tell”.
(And be savvy at breaking any such rules that they have mastered).











Shadow of the Colossus (2005).
With such grammar in hand, a visual storyteller can craft a character’s point-of-view.










Artists and designers want to communicate in order to question and persuade.
Two of the class’s primary themes are the player’s experiences of control and discovery.
Let’s get into that…










Narrative Roles
Your first three assignments are framed by a sequence of narrative roles.
Player’s experiences are shaped by the role they are given – what the player can and does do.
This class will study four such roles with pragmatism:
three provide constraints for assignments during our first 10 weeks, while The Entrant clarifies the transition from discovery to control.










The Protagonist

Horizon Zero Dawn (2017).
First, What is a main character?
The most common cinematic storytelling framework centers around the protagonist, the pursuit of most professional storytellers from all mediums.











Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1983).
The Protagonist

Get Out (2017).
The Protagonist faces danger or crisis often embodied in other characters. As the player struggles against antagonists (and sometimes themselves), their relationship to the concept of control provides the conduit for our empathy, and by extension, how we engage the story’s themes.

Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

Ghost in the Shell (1995).











Genshin Impact (2020).

God of War (2018).
We feel empathy towards protagonists. This dynamic operates as a cycle found in popular literature and Hollywood films: we get to know our character’s internal reality by seeing the choices they make under stress.

Final Fantasy VII Remake (2020).

The Last of Us Part II (2020).










Once we understand what they want, we anticipate what they might do, and we also witness good and bad things happening to them.
Therefore, the story is composed of a range of strong and mild surprises.
The cycle repeats with different or progressed dilemmas.

Bones and All (2022).










Sometimes the character must discover their internal reality in order to control their external one.

The Matrix (1999).











Sound of Metal (2019).
Other times, after they fail to control their external world, they discover insight: perhaps they learn that they were not struggling against others, but against themselves.











Baba Is You (2019).
No doubt, Game Design includes providing players the experiences of discovery and control.










But narrative games complicate the protagonist paradigm.
In such video games, there are two main characters: the protagonist and the player.
The narrative films we watch center on their protagonist. The narrative games we study can have a protagonist too (the player character), but they also make room for another main character: the player, and the story created by what the player does.
This is why our early assignments isolate four player roles, framing storytelling through what the player can and does do.










The Investigator

Tacoma (2017).
Assignment 1: The Investigator










The Investigator

Firewatch (2016).

The Investigator role embraces much of what we know from the detective and mystery genres of literature and cinema.
The character searches for clues and engages other characters to discover the story.
The game’s plot is the player’s attempt at gathering information, and the story is the resulting sequence of events we mentally, and retrospectively, stitch together in our minds.

L.A. Noire (2011).

Chinatown (1974).










The Investigator role provides an excellent framework for environmental storytelling.











Dark Souls III (2016), Firelink Shrine — facing the five thrones of the Lords of Cinder.
Dark Souls III is not focused on The Investigator, but it repeatedly creates Investigator experiences. The player reads item descriptions and messages, inspects objects, listens to NPCs, and studies architecture and remains to reconstruct what happened.
The environmental designer embeds clues, events, and characters in the world. They are part level designer, architect, and teller of tales.











*Installation at The Broad, Los Angeles
The Investigator
We find such storytelling in a myriad of forms, including themed entertainment (such as Disneyland), escape rooms, alternate reality games, and museums.










The Investigator

Global Conflicts: Palestine.
Because The Investigator primarily discovers (rather than controls), this role provides straightforward mechanics for real-world topics.











Her Story (2015) — a story discovered in the past tense.
Games featuring the other three roles tell their stories in the present tense.
But The Investigator discovers the story that happened in the past.










Plot and story
Detective fiction gives us the cleanest version of this distinction, and it is worth naming precisely.

The plot is the order in which the player encounters the investigation.
The story is the underlying sequence of events, assembled retrospectively.

Chinatown and The Maltese Falcon both work this way. The detective changes very little in the world. The clues, the motives, and the relationships are all in place before the film begins — what changes over the course of it is comprehension.
Designing for The Investigator means designing the plot: deciding what the player finds, and in what order, so that the story assembles itself in their head.










What visual techniques might be handy for your Investigator project?
How about mechanics?

reads, looks, finds, collects











The Traveler

Everything (2017).
Assignment 2: The Traveler











Twin Peaks: The Return (2017) — the Red Room as a labyrinth to be navigated.
The Traveler
The Traveler explores in order to discover situations and events.
Often, they navigate labyrinths.











Zork.
The Traveler’s power is to find their path and to bear witness to the story.











The Unfinished Swan (2012).
That path can be narrative or spatial (or both).











A Short Hike (2019).
The Traveler’s journey ponders free will.










Maze and Labyrinth
We use these two words in a specific way:

A maze is what the word normally evokes — a puzzle of pathways, designed to be solved.
A labyrinth is a maze plus meaning. It is architecture built to carry a story or a metaphor.

The Traveler moves through a labyrinth, not a maze. The difference is whether the space is something to solve or something to undergo.
Umberto Eco separates mazes by how they branch:

Unicursal — one winding path, no choices. You cannot get lost, because there is only one route.
Multicursal — branches, dead ends, and decisions at every intersection.
Network — every point can connect to many others. No fixed start, no fixed end.











What visual techniques might be handy for your Traveler project?
How about mechanics?

walks, chooses, sees, explores











The Entrant
Situated Player Role 3: The Entrant
The Entrant has arrived at a boundary.
Unlike The Traveler, who moves through space as an interpretive act, The Entrant confronts a blocked passage. Progress is possible — but only by satisfying conditions.
The player asks: How does this world work?











Uncharted.
The Entrant reads what is present, tests what the system accepts or rejects, and gradually learns the rules governing passage.
The threshold might be a locked door, a puzzle room, a boss, a border, or a bureaucratic procedure.











Portal (2007) — the chamber itself is a spatial threshold.
In Portal, passage is not blocked by a conventional locked door. The player must reorganize space by creating a non-Euclidean pathway through the chamber.
The player does not merely find the path, as The Traveler might. They must understand and manipulate the room’s system to make passage possible.











Papers, Please (2013) — a bureaucratic threshold.
Not every threshold is architectural. In Papers, Please, the player becomes the threshold: inspecting documents, applying changing rules, and deciding who may cross the border.
The act of accepting or rejecting passage becomes the story.










The Shift to Control
The Entrant marks the framework’s major shift from discovery toward control.
Agency is no longer expressed merely through movement or interpretation, but by demonstrating alignment with the system’s demands.










The Entrant’s loop: L.O.P.
The puzzle-platformer Inside (2016) consistently manifests a repeatable three-step loop: Legibility, Opportunity, and Performance.

Inside (2016) — Legibility.
Legibility: See what matters. The player recognizes the barrier and identifies the interactive components in the room.











Inside (2016) — Opportunity.
Opportunity: Imagine the solution. By experimenting with individual mechanics, the player imagines how the components might be configured or sequenced.











Inside (2016) — Performance.
Performance: Test the idea. The player attempts to carry out the imagined solution. The system accepts or rejects the performance.
The Investigator learns what happened. The Traveler reaches the boundary. The Entrant tests whether understanding and action are sufficient to cross it.
The threshold does more than halt progress: it defines the player’s relationship to the world and its rules.










What visual techniques make a threshold legible?
How do the mechanics let the player imagine and perform a solution?

reads, tests, configures, performs











The Dreamer

John Tenniel’s illustration for Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865).
Assignment 3: The Dreamer











Humanity (2023).

Inception (2010).
The Dreamer

Inside (2016).
The Dreamer strives to control their environment, but unlike The Entrant — who confronts a material reality — The Dreamer confronts a symbolic one.
The world expresses an internal state, and the player must interpret that expression in order to act.
The player asks: What does this world express?

Baba Is You (2019).

Braid (2008).











The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
With this role, the world is rich and vibrant.
Like in expressionistic cinema from early 20th century, the world holds the intrigue.











The Witness (2016).
At the level of mechanics, a Dreamer game may resemble an Entrant game: both can use puzzles.
The distinction is not whether the player solves a puzzle, but whether the puzzle also functions as metaphor.











Alice in Wonderland (Disney, 1951).
Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland provides an excellent entry point for the shift between The Entrant and The Dreamer.
The Entrant approach: Alice tries a key in a locked door. The problem follows grounded logic, but she is too large to pass through.
The Dreamer approach: she must drink from a bottle and eat cake, changing her body and accepting the dream logic of the world.
The Entrant’s threshold demands mastery of how the world works. The Dreamer’s threshold demands recognition of what the world expresses.











Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022).
_We take on the same task as our character –
interpreting images in order to take the next steps. 

_Such images are both symbolic and a piece of the puzzle.











Papo & Yo (2012).
The task of interpreting what the thing can do…
How is that connected to interpreting what it means?











Humanity (2023).
But it is not only the puzzle pieces that are symbolic, but (like with our own dreams), the overall experience is worth interpreting.











Paprika (2006) — a world that is explicitly an externalized dream.
In some cases, the worlds are not merely dream-like but are explicitly externalized dreams. 











Inside (2016).
We might not have access to The Dreamer’s thoughts in the way we expect from a traditional protagonist.
In this case, the player character is like a blank canvas for what we are thinking, therefore the avatar’s visual rendering might lack detail.










The Alice Shift
Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland shows the exact moment The Entrant becomes The Dreamer. Alice is stuck in a hallway, behind a locked door only ten inches high.

The Entrant approach — rationality. She tries the key in the locks. It fits the small door, but she cannot fit through it. She reasons about keys and doors as material things.
The Dreamer approach — surrealism. She goes back to the table and finds a bottle labeled “DRINK ME.” To get through, she has to accept the logic the world is offering and change her own body to match it.

The Entrant’s threshold asks the player to master how the world works. The Dreamer’s threshold asks them to recognize what the world is expressing.
The L.O.P. loop still runs here — but legibility becomes the hard part rather than the first step. In Papo & Yo, the puzzles are a metaphor for living with an alcoholic parent. The player still solves them; the meaning is in what solving them reveals. The mechanics are the language.










What visual techniques might be handy for your Dreamer project?
How about mechanics?

Instructor notesinterprets, connects, transforms, configures











Roles Overlap

Death Stranding (2019).
HOLD ON!
Most games – especially AAA games – oscillate among roles.
Players Can
investigate, travel, cross thresholds, solve, and interpret










How would you describe other playable roles?
In…
Procedural Narrative
(Tabletop) Role Playing Games (both the DM and the players)
*What else?
_*This is your challenge going forward. To become a games scholar _.

534/Lectures/Week-2.1---The-Value-of-Unc.title: Week 2.1 - The Value of Uncertainty
534/Lectures/Week-2.1---The-Value-of-Unc.content:
Three topics we’ll be juggling for Project 1

Investigator, Protagonist, Visual Grammar











Sources
The Value of Uncertainty
Four Authors – philosophers and psychologist
aeon.co/essays/use-uncertainty-to-leverage-the-power-of-your-predictive-brain










keywords
Certainty, uncertainty, volatility, surprise, explore, information, solution, control










Three Stages
3 Stages


Expected Uncertainty


Unexpected Uncertainty


Volatility












Concepts
First, let’s focus on some concepts.










Mental Model


What a person believes or thinks they know about a system


A person’s expectations of an external reality, a simplified version


Constructed from their past experiences













A retail site interrupts the visit with an email-capture pop-up.

A newsletter page and its navigation rail.
Because of the pop up, clicking the back button takes them back to google, the actual first page.










Predictive Processing
Human brains are designed to minimize their own average surprise (prediction error) during
real-life exchanges with the world.










Predictive Processing: Peter’s Preemptive Summary
When we find ourselves at a prediction level at “medium” as opposed to “excellent” or “terrible”, we respond by seeking more information for our model – compelling us to be open to learning and exploring.
This can be fun. (Careful with that word, “fun”).


                  
                  Instructor shares 
                  
                

This is Peter’s interpretation and take. Including coupling learning with fun.












We probe the world in ways that aim to reveal just where the key uncertainties lie, so that by future actions they can resolve them and move on.
We seek new information and engage in complex rituals such as art…whose role is to safely reveal and stress-test our own deepest assumptions.










epistemic (knowledge-seeking) ----- discovery
pragmatic (puzzle-solving) ----------- control










1. Expected Uncertainty
Expected uncertainty is experienced whenever we know the weak spots in our information, and we can take action accordingly (i.e. control).
We are equipped to ‘think things through’ in advance of acting because we have a workable mental model.










An example: registration
You want to enroll in a popular class that has 2 sections, but maybe 3.


The 8am (Bad) — T/Th. Undesirable time. Fills last, but it does fill.


The Monday night (Ok) — 6–9pm, one three-hour block. This is adequate.


The rumored Wednesday noon (Great) — drops between your two other classes. No extra trip to campus. Ideal.












The night before
You don’t know how fast the Monday (the OK one) night fills.
But you know the 8am (Bad) goes last. You know roughly how last year went. You wonder if the noon section (Great) is only a rumor.
You don’t know what will happen, but you know exactly where your ignorance is.










The plan is clean
Running “if I take the Monday night (OK), I still have a seat, and I can watch for noon (Great)” in your head, before touching the portal.
→ Thinking is an action. It harvests information from the model you already have.
And the plan is correct. Switching is free and easy, so grabbing a fallback costs you nothing. You end up with a seat either way, and the noon section stays in reach.










Precision
“We were told a third might open” — by whom?
A department admin’s email and a group-chat rumor are the same information at different confidence.
The confidence decides how much of the plan you build around it.










2. Unexpected Uncertainty
Unexpected uncertainty typically occurs when the environment (the rule structure) changes without our being in a position to predict that change.
This might be my cue to move into exploratory mode.
Predictive brains expect control and, if it fails, they drive learning.
We know there is a pattern. We just have to discover it.










The rule changes
You take the Monday night.  And it fills.
Then the registrar posts a new drop/add rule — you have to drop a class before you can add another.  There is not longer a ‘swapping’ option.
You know from past experience that dropping takes the system 5 to 30 minutes to complete.
Your plan wasn’t wrong. It was made under different rules.










Now it’s a dilemma
Explore vs. exploit. There was no tradeoff yesterday, because enrolling was free. This new delay in changing sections - a period of minutes in which you are enrolled in nothing -  manufactures one.










What you do next
Email the advisor. Ask people who registered yesterday whether the lock hit them. Check whether it applies to waitlist auto-enrolls.
That’s the learning rate going up.  You attempt discovery.
The registrar has rules. They’re just not published.










3. Volatility
Volatility is subtly different: it names a situation in which the frequency of changes in the rules or situation are themselves rapidly changing.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.










Registration, continued
Wednesday, the noon (Great) section is added. Just before you drop your OK section, the Great section is pulled.  Phew.
Thursday it’s back with a cap of 10 students.
Friday there’s a rumor of another one.










You can’t learn a rate
There’s no strategy to form, because the thing you’d form it about won’t hold still.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.
You either freeze — stay in the Monday night (Ok), stop checking, let the noon section go —
or refresh the portal every ten minutes for four days and learn nothing.
That’s the tell: your choices stopped paying. What’s left is only how you cope with that.










Volatility
With unexpected uncertainty (#2), our strategies can work – in our mode of learning and openness.
But with volatility, our strategies are suspect. People and animals find this situation extremely uncomfortable.










We recognize that our ability to discover is weak, therefore we have no control.










Marvel Snap
The same three stages, in a game










Marvel Snap — Expected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — the collection screen.
The Player,
“I don’t know exactly what is going to happen. But I am quite oriented.”










Marvel Snap — Unexpected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — building a deck.

*Marvel Snap
A new ability - a card whose On Reveal ability changes the location itself.*










Marvel Snap — Volatility
Our cards are taken away
and we are forced into
a “Redemption Round”


                  
                  Instructor notes 
                  
                

I made this up. I don’t know if I’m playing AI, if this round will win my cards back or if there’s no connection.
There’s no example in Marvel Snap because volatility is bad, so you’re not going to see it in a game like this.












Art
Art has expected uncertainty (#1),
and unexpected uncertainty (#2).
Our predictive models are encountered as objects →
we understand our own expectations.










This reveal can be a way of materializing and confronting our own high-level assumptions, about self, world and other, but doing so in a framework that steps back from daily concerns.











Certain and uncertain, against pretend (practice) and real.

I challenge you to devise over the next 10 years what characterizes your era (century) and your game making.












Modernism and Modernity

Salvador Dalí, The Persistence of Memory (1931).
Modernism

Farago: “Modernism an umbrella term to cover a focus on innovation that occurred across almost all forms of human expression in the early 20th century, most notably in the fields of literature, music, art, film and literature”.












Modernity

Harold Lloyd hanging from the clock in Safety Last! (1923).

The economic and technological growth of the period between 1870 and 1970 — was fueled by unique and unrepeatable innovations (electricity, sanitation, the combustion engine) whose successors (like information technology) have not had the same impact.
Before we get to cool art, modernity gave us:
Phone calls. Sewage treatment. Light at night. Travel by car, etc.











Novelty and Difficulty











The First Condition — Difficulty

Difficulty: Configuration
Difficulty: Interpretation (we’re talking about this one)

Not Bloodborne difficulty, but…
… the task of interpretation
Not looking for a solution, but an interpretation.

Pre-Modern(ism)
Easy to Interpret.

















Your job as an artist was no longer to glorify the king or the church, nor to imitate as faithfully as possible the appearance of the outside world.












You think AI is upsetting for artists today?

Camera confronted realism.
The camera inspired artists to move on.











Interpretation Before Video Games
Before Video Games, We Interpreted Art

Marcel Duchamp, Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 (1912).

Albert Einstein.

*Sigmund Freud.

Before your time (20th century)
Before video games, we did:
INTERPRETATION
I like to think about what was happening in culture when a medium “comes out”. I’m not comparing cinema to games. I’m offering that a medium’s timing and context can be revealing.
Cinema was affected by people such as Freud, Duchamp, and Einstein.
Further, the mind is a puzzle that warrants interpretation.
What a wonderful time for cinema to “come out”.












Picasso
Cubism
In the 20th Century, your point of view….

Cubism embraced: the artist’s starting point was the recognition that there was no true perspective from which we could objectively view and understand what we were looking at.












The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari

Expressionism on the other hand makes a choice with perspective. Nevertheless, it admits to being subjective.












Battleship Potemkin (1925) — montage.
Cinema, as a recorded medium provided a new perspective on time.










The Kuleshov Effect
1.8

The Kuleshov effect.









Paris, I Love You (29:52)

Paris, I Love You — a near-expressionless face.
Kuleshov Effect










Time, Space, and Point of View

Marcel Duchamp, Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 (1912).
Multiple Angles (Space)
But Also
Multiple Moments (Time)

Painting could represent multiple moments, sure, but cinema ran with such possibilities.












Moving clocks run slower than stationary ones.

Speaking of time………………………………………………..Einstein!


Einstein and 4th dimension. –Time is relative. “Moving clocks are slower than stationary ones.”










The Mind as a Puzzle

The Mind
The Conscious and Unconscious
(Let’s interpret: what is the main character thinking?)

Freud’s is an essential figure in the 20th Century. We can thank him and Carl Yung for psychoanalysis, and perhaps by extension, therapy. Most of his specific ideas are passe, for example his interpretations themselves, such as penis envy and so on.
 
But something rings true with his distinction and relationship between the conscious and unconscious mind. The mind, a person’s thoughts, memories and personality, are a puzzle to be solved, to be interpreted. Let us ponder if the unconscious explains most of our behavior.
And next: it takes work to get to know ourselves. We have repressed thoughts, from prior experiences. They cause unexpected behavior, and dreams, no doubt.
 
This is familiar. Movies seem to work the same way. This is rich stuff for the filmmaker. As viewers, it seems to be our role to interpret the motivation of the characters, the possibilities for outcomes, and indeed what the film means.











[In traditional stories], the dramatic question [gets answered at the end]. We’ll leave the story with that lovely emotional sense that something, perhaps just beyond the level of conscious comprehension, has been completed.
Modernist stories are different.
Storr, Will. The Science of Storytelling: Why Stories Make Us Human and How to Tell Them Better (pp. 128-129). Abrams Press. Kindle Edition.


                  
                  Instructor notes 
                  
                

Read aloud:
Modernist stories are different. Whilst they’re built from the same dance between surface drama and subconscious change, their causes and effects are often left ambiguous. Character change occurs, but it’s less clear how these changes are being triggered by the drama and what message we’re supposed to glean from them. More space is left for the reader to insert their own interpretations into the text.
Franz Kafka’s short story ‘The Passenger’ shows an enigmatic movement of cause and effect between consciousness and subconscious. It tells of a man on a tram feeling uncertain about himself and his place in the world. He becomes lost, for a moment, in the abstract physical details of a woman waiting to disembark – the position of her hands, the shape of her nose, the shadow her ear makes against her skull. These conscious observations trigger something deep in his subconscious. He asks, ‘How is it that she is not astonished at herself, that she keeps her mouth closed, and expresses nothing of any wonderment?’ The reader is invited to ponder how one level connects to the other and thereby bring them into harmony.














**

Cinema does: The mind is a puzzle











Cinema is the artform of time, dreams, and point of view.

Dreams (More On This Another Week)

Labyrinths










What a Labyrinth Is
Labyrinths are expressive mazes. That is, they are vehicles for a story, or they are metaphors themselves.

(This is Peter’s definition)




























MainstreamLabyrinthsGaining powerLosing powerFree willOr experiencing not having it










Three Kinds — Unicursal, Multicursal, Network

Unicursal
Multicursal
Network


Umberto Eco:
unicursal – when you go in, you are bound to reach the center, and back out. Unicursal isn’t so intimidating because of this, if it weren’t for the Minotaur. If it were unfolded, it would be a line, a straight path.
 
multicursal (maze) – provides alternative paths, all leading to a dead end, apart from one which leads to an exit. If it were unfolded, it would be a tree, or as we know, branches.
You make mistakes, and back up and try again.
 
network – each point can be connected to any other point, which makes it possible to travel around forever. But a network cannot be unfolded like into a line or tree. You keep going around inside. The illusion of freedom comes from the fact that the network is so large that it seems to have no limits.
 
A dictionary, and therefore the spoken word, is network shaped. A dictionary tells us that a dog is a four-legged animal which barks, but then you have to go and find out the meaning of the word’s animal, four-legged, and bark and each of these terms leads to another and so on for infinity without you realizing that you are moving in a circle and will never get out.
 
Eco believes knowledge is like this and of course, the internet.
 

What genre and stories lend themselves? Uncharted is unicursal; many game are multicursal, perhaps even uncharted with dead ends;
network perhaps is open world.













**

*The Minotaur.

In Greek mythology, the minotaur is a monster with a bull’s head and a man’s body, which was confined in a labyrinth











Labyrinths and the Self
We engage the labyrinth with a logical mindset, to solve it. But we end up learning about ourselves.










Labyrinths and the Unconscious
The Minotaur represents the part of the unconscious that we fear. The labyrinth represents the journey we take to understand ourselves. Doesn’t this sound familiar?
We’re not sure we want to go there: the minotaur is what we hope we don’t find.
In Greek mythology, the Minotaur was put in there to keep him from getting out.










Labyrinths and Insight
Again, we engage the labyrinth with a logical mindset, to solve the external. But we end up learning about ourselves – the internal.

Units: 4

Lunch Section: Tue, Thu, 1:00–3:20 pm
Go To Schedule
Instructor: Peter Brinson
Student Assistant: Yinuo Chen
Student Assistant: George Zou
Course Description
Is Life A Story or a Game?
We will study and practice how narrative video games express meaning, make topics and themes playable, and how they uniquely invoke the player’s emotions.
Artists want to communicate in order to question and persuade. What does this mean for narrative game design?
This course has four overarching topics.

Visual Grammar
Storytelling: The Player Character’s Role and Situation
Worldbuilding: Playable Worlds Expressive Through The Space’s Edges
Pragmatic Practices for Creators

The first two topics focus on two principles at a narrative designer’s disposal: the language of the moving image and the video game player’s role. The third considers the game world itself: how its limits, rules, and responses can express meaning through play.
The fourth topic — pragmatic creative practices — explores how successful artists imagine compelling ideas, execute on a small scale, and participate in a culture of critique and creative growth.
Grammar
We study the visual grammar of cinema and how it provides a valuable starting point for how video games tell stories. We consider how color, lighting, composition, montage, and cinematography shape our attention in order to communicate.
Cinema language is also sonic. Audio design represents one of the most powerful and flexible of the narrative game designer’s tools, and film audio shows us much of what is possible in video games.
Playable Roles
Mainstream storytelling features a character who attempts to control their reality. They want something, and we anticipate how they might get it. What comes next: surprises. Some surprises are small, some are large.
With this canon in hand, we continue with mainstream alternatives, such as stories that do not conclude with the protagonist attaining power, but instead, stories that close with an emphasis on the character (and player) discovering insight and understanding.
Further, all narrative games complicate the protagonist paradigm as there are two main characters: the protagonist and the player.
In summary, we study how narrative game situations inform what the player can and does do.
Worldbuilding
Situations also provide our way into worldbuilding. As the player moves from one situation to the next, they meet the world, learn its rules, experience its responses, and discover what lies at or beyond its edges.
Rather than treating a world as setting or backstory—or pursuing size and exhaustive lore—we focus on making playable worlds feel coherent, inhabited, and expressive through their limits.
Creative Practices
Throughout the semester we will learn pragmatic creative practices. How do successful artists imagine and articulate their nascent ideas? What techniques maximize the goal of tackling compelling projects that student teams can reasonably create?
The ultimate outcome of this course is to prepare you for subsequent classes in which you will be expected to quickly imagine compelling game ideas and then make them.

A Perspective
Stories embody two apparently conflicting impulses — to connect us to something real at the same time inviting us to believe in magic. The novelist Marcel Theroux frames the paradox of stories this way. He says that storytelling wobbles between authenticity and enchantment. On one hand, we want stories to feel like they must be real for someone, and on the other, we want to engage the possibility of what cannot exist.

All lectures and discussions are for the sake of shaping and inspiring the course’s assignments.

Another Perspective
Insert the word “story” in the place of “book” and consider what’s happening today. From David Bell: “It is here, with this question of engagement, that the comparison between the Enlightenment and A.I.’s supposed ‘second Enlightenment’ breaks down and reveals something important about the latter’s limits and dangers. When readers interact imaginatively with a book, they are still following the book’s lead, attempting to answer the book’s questions, responding to the book’s challenges and therefore putting their own convictions at risk.”

Learning Objectives
Visual and Interactive Storytelling

Describe how visual storytelling approaches build subtext and theme with an emphasis on point-of-view.
Understand color theory and lighting in order to compose communicative visual designs.
Create story stakes, pressure, and growth for your characters.
Compare how cinematic and interactive storytelling techniques express change and contrast. For example, evaluate how video editing creates montage in order to understand relevant approaches in game language.
Analyze the arc of experience in films and games.
Discuss how prior art research inspires your work.

Digital Media Development

Construct interactive worlds in the Unity game engine (literacy).
Translate photography and video camera operation to game camera principles.
Understand the essential components of 3D models, including materials, textures, and meshes, in order to incorporate them in-game.
Create rich and meaningful sound designs.

Production Methods

Explain how self-direction couples with shared creative visions.
Give and take critique.
Use ideation, brainstorming, and prototyping approaches.

PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.title: Situated Player Role 1 - The Investigator, World as Evidence
PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.content:
Summarized in: Situated Player Roles
Next: Situated Player Role 2: The Traveler

The Investigator probes a world to reconstruct the events that shaped its present condition. The player has arrived late: the events have transpired.
Through environmental storytelling, the Investigator asks, “What happened?”
Discovery and Analysis
Discovery means attending closely to what the world presents. For the Investigator, this happens through mechanics such as:

Exploring and examining spaces
Using maps to connect locations
Reading notes and listening to recordings
Questioning NPCs

These mechanics give the player control over movement, attention, and access to evidence. But that control serves discovery: the player uses what they find to reconstruct past events.
Success might be measured by the system, but it is also intrinsic; progress comes from learning enough of the world’s internal consistency to read its evidence. Understanding how natural forces behave, how people and places connect, and how technology functions helps the player assemble that evidence into a causal history.
With this understanding in place, the player can begin to speculate — quietly imagining the parts of the world and story they cannot directly access.
Plot vs. Story
Detective fiction and film noir provide the canonical examples for this role. In films like The Maltese Falcon (1941) and Chinatown (1974), the detective’s actions arise in response to a mystery already present in the world. From the start, clues, motives, and relationships are in place, but not yet understood. We anticipate what the detective is seeking and follow as they discover what those clues mean.


The Plot: The sequence in which the detective (and the audience) experiences the investigation.
The Story: The underlying events as they are retrospectively sequenced through the investigation.

Video Game Examples
Return of the Obra Dinn

Return of the Obra Dinn mirrors detective fiction perfectly. An insurance inspector investigates a ship mutiny by examining audio fragments and suspended moments in time to match evidence to causal chains.

Gone Home

Gone Home demonstrates that Investigator stories are not limited to crime. The game invites the player to piece together a coming-of-age narrative embedded in the family’s new home.
Its follow-up, Tacoma, translates this to science fiction, featuring 3D recordings that reconstruct a tragedy on a space station.

Her Story

Her Story proves this role doesn’t necessarily explore physical space. It confines the player to a database, where discovery comes from searching records and noting contradictions across time.

Disco Elysium

Disco Elysium simultaneously attends to the present and the past. It mixes retroactive reconstruction with a living present: the player starts by investigating past events and soon must parse competing political ideologies and social forces presently active in the town.

Multiple Roles in a Single Game

AAA games contain multiple Situated Player Roles. The Investigator — examining an interior in Skyrim, probing a map’s lore in Elden Ring, or conversing with a character in The Outer Worlds — likely sits off the main line of action, but remains essential to the game’s storytelling.
For instance, Alan Wake 2 manifests all four roles: Saga reconstructs ritual murders from evidence; both protagonists travel through realities as events unfold around them; Saga discovers and performs rituals that open passages between realities; and Alan rewrites scenes, turning authorship into a mechanic that transforms the world.

Allegory

Perhaps the most straightforward encapsulation of The Investigator can be found in a short animated film, La Maison en Petits Cubes. Neither a detective nor adventurer, the protagonist is an old man alone in an elemental world. He descends floor by floor into a flooded, impossibly tall and multi-storied house; each level is a lived period, a memory recovered through exploration. This short film captures how spaces can represent a life and how descending into them is an act of remembering.
www.youtube.com/watch
Where games make The Investigator most salient is in their system of knowing: understanding is earned through what the player chooses to examine, read, listen to, and connect. This role treats narrative as discoverable and stable, rewarding players who slow down, take notes, and update comprehension as new evidence appears.
Next: Situated Player Role 2: The Traveler

PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.title: Situated Player Role 2 - The Traveler, World as Presence
PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.content:
Summarized in: Situated Player Roles
Previous: Situated Player Role 1: The Investigator | Next: Situated Player Role 3: The Entrant

The Traveler explores a world in the present tense. Like the Investigator, the Traveler is oriented toward discovery. But where the Investigator treats what is present as evidence of events beyond reach, the Traveler discovers meaning through movement, attention, and what is encountered along the way.
A familiar philosophical riddle captures this logic: if a tree falls in the woods and no one is there to hear it, does it make a sound? For the Traveler, the answer is no. In this role, narrative is constituted by presence. What The Traveler sees, passes through, and confronts is the story. Movement and attention are the Traveler’s central mechanics: where the player walks, when they pause, and what they stop to see or hear determine what the world reveals. The player asks, “What is this experience?”
The Labyrinth

The Traveler’s world is a labyrinth — whether explicit or implicit. Examples range from a literal maze of walls and corridors to a setting that produces the experience of a maze without explicitly presenting one.
Story Without the Cutscene

A useful early touchstone is Half-Life (1998), which famously dissolved the cutscene. Narrative events occur during play, around the player. These moments mark an early and influential shift toward a Traveler-oriented understanding of game narrative.
Subjectivity and Uncertainty

When a game centers on the Traveler role, it stands as the most experimental of the Situated Player Roles. Its values run against the dominant tendencies of mainstream game design — the drive toward efficiency and clear outcomes — by asking the player to tolerate absence as part of the experience.
When we describe a video game as “difficult,” we usually mean it demands dexterity, strategy, and precise execution. The Traveler is difficult in a different way. It leans into the challenge of interpretation. In this way, the Traveler aligns with the ambitions of many painters, experimental musicians, and filmmakers: to create an encounter that invites interpretation rather than resolution.
Disobedience

The Path (by Tale of Tales) embodies this rebellious spirit. The game gives a clear instruction — “And Stay on the Path” — but the instruction is a deceit. The meaningful experience requires disobedience. Off the path the player might:

find a girl in a white dress standing beside a wolf at a piano
encounter a silent campfire deep in the woods
come across an abandoned structure that suggests a situation but refuses explanation

These encounters are not framed as steps toward progress. The player moves through the labyrinth without reducing it to a problem to be identified and solved.
Cinematic Point of View

This emphasis on point of view connects the Traveler strongly to 20th-century cinema, deeply concerned with subjectivity and presence. “One take” films invite the viewer in as a silent and invisible character: Hitchcock’s Rope (1948), Russian Ark (2002), and The Way Things Go (1987) all position the viewer within a continuous present. These are an exception, and yet provide a powerful reference for 3D games, where the “one take” is the norm.
The continuous take emphasizes the viewer as a proximate witness, responsible for orienting themselves, choosing where to look, and forming their own judgments.

Like the Sleepwalker
In Visionary Film, film scholar P. Adams Sitney says the avant-garde cinema protagonist “wanders through a potent environment toward a climactic scene of self-realization. The stages of his progress are often marked by what he sees along his path rather than what he does.”

In Twin Peaks, Agent Cooper does not choose his path through the Red Room. He is there to experience its confusing, shifting logic.
Control in Service of Discovery

A particularly pure interactive example appears at the opening of Giant Sparrow’s Unfinished Swan. The world begins as blank white nothing. The player can only walk and throw black paint, gradually revealing the contours of a three-dimensional environment. These simple actions literally bring the world into perceptual existence. The player acts upon the world by walking and throwing paint, but that control serves discovery by making the environment perceptible.
Free Will

The Stanley Parable is the defining Traveler game. As the player navigates its office corridors, the narrator describes Stanley’s actions in real time, anticipating our choices and framing them before we make them. Play consists of selecting one path after another until navigation itself becomes a question about agency. Each turn tests whether choice is freedom or performance.
The Traveler Among the Other Roles

When a game is structured largely around the Traveler role, it takes on this experimental character. More commonly, however, the Traveler appears within large-scale commercial games — particularly open world games, which routinely integrate three or four of the Situated Player Roles. The Traveler typically occupies the spaces between roles defined by higher degrees of control (see Situated Player Role 3: The Entrant and Situated Player Role 4: The Dreamer). Traversing regions, moving between towns, or crossing large-scale spaces provides rhythm and interpretive breathing room.
For Our Needs, Terminology: Maze and Labyrinth
For our understanding of The Traveler, we use the term labyrinth in a specific sense, defined as a subset of the maze:

A Maze is what the word naturally evokes — a puzzle of pathways designed to be solved.
A Labyrinth is a maze plus signification. It is architecture for a story or metaphor.

Structure: Three Types of Mazes

In Umberto Eco’s Et in Labyrintho Ego, labyrinths are spatial structures described by how their paths connect. For the Situated Player Roles, we can apply all three of his types to the distinction above.

Unicursal — A single winding path with no branches or choices; you cannot get lost because there is only one route.
Multicursal — A branching structure with choices and dead ends; you must decide at intersections, and wrong decisions lead to retracing your steps.
Network — A web in which each point can potentially connect to any other. It cannot be unfolded into a single route or branching tree, and the traveler can continue circulating within it indefinitely.

If the Investigator treats narrative as evidence to be reconstructed, the Traveler treats narrative as something encountered — moment by moment — shaped by what is witnessed along the way.

PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.title: Situated Player Role 3 - The Entrant, World as Threshold
PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.content:
Summarized in: Situated Player Roles
Previous: Situated Player Role 2: The Traveler | Next: Situated Player Role 4: The Dreamer

The Entrant has arrived at a boundary. Unlike the Investigator, who researches the past, or the Traveler, who moves through space as an interpretive act, the Entrant confronts a blocked passage. Progress is possible — but only by satisfying conditions.
These thresholds appear as gates, locked doors, guarded borders, or rituals. The player reads what is present in the space, tests what the system accepts or rejects, and gradually learns the rules governing passage. The room is a puzzle that compels the player to ask, “How does this world work?”
The Shift to Control
The shift toward control is visible in what the mechanics ask the player to do. In The Legend of Zelda (1986), the player finds a key and uses it to change a locked door into an open passage. In Breath of the Wild (2017), the player discovers how the shrine’s components behave, then reconfigures the room by rotating gears with Magnesis or freezing water with Cryonis.
Types of Thresholds
Spatial Threshold

In Portal (2007), each chamber presents an exit isolated by its architecture and hazards. The player creates a non-Euclidean route to it; once they pass through, the story continues.
Boss Threshold

In Demon’s Souls, each Archstone path culminates in a powerful demon. The player studies the boss’s patterns and weaknesses, then defeats it to open the way forward. These victories advance the larger quest: becoming the Slayer of Demons and returning the Old One to slumber.
Bureaucratic Threshold

The Entrant does not always confront a physical challenge. Papers, Please (2013) approaches the threshold from the other side. The player does not seek passage but administers it: inspecting documents, applying rules, and deciding who may pass.
The Entrant’s Loop: L.O.P.
The Entrant operates through a repeatable three-step loop: L.O.P. — Legibility, Opportunity, and Performance.
The puzzle-platformer Inside (2016) consistently manifests L.O.P.

Legibility (“See what matters.”) — The player attends closely to the space, recognizing the barrier and identifying its interactive components.


Opportunity (“Imagine the solution.”) — By testing individual mechanics, the player discovers how the components could be configured or sequenced. Solutions exist first as speculations; opportunities arrive as epiphanies.


Performance (“Test the idea.”) — The player acts upon the world, manipulating its components and testing whether the imagined solution works.
L.O.P. structures the Entrant’s movement from discovery toward control. Legibility and Opportunity build understanding; Performance uses that understanding to act upon the world. The threshold asks the player to notice, learn, and do what passage requires.
The Investigator reconstructs the events that produced the present situation. The Traveler experiences events as they unfold. The Entrant discovers what the present situation permits, acts to change it, and passes onward.
For the Entrant, overcoming a threshold allows the story to continue. The Dreamer, the next role, connects action and story differently: The Entrant advances through the story. The Dreamer performs it.
Next: Situated Player Role 4: The Dreamer

PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.title: Situated Player Role 4 - The Dreamer, World as Enigma
PBOH/Design/Storytelling/Situated-Player.content:
Summarized in: Situated Player Roles
Previous: Situated Player Role 3: The Entrant
The Dreamer acts within a world whose mechanics go beyond governing progress: they express an emotional, thematic, or psychological dimension of the story. The player discovers how the rules work while acting within them, and those same actions carry metaphorical meaning. The Dreamer asks, “What does this world express?”
The “Alice” Shift: Progression as Expression
We can see the shift from The Entrant to The Dreamer in Chapters 1 and 2 of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland. Alice confronts a door about fifteen inches high. The key fits, but she is too large to pass through.
The Entrant’s L.O.P. loop structures what follows:

Legibility: Alice recognizes the relationship among the key, the door, and her size.
Opportunity: The “DRINK ME” bottle and “EAT ME” cake suggest that her size can be changed.
Performance: Alice drinks, eats, and tests her changing body against the threshold.

Within the larger context of Wonderland, the story primes us to expect its dreamlike rules and actions to carry meaning, allowing Alice’s solutions to function as metaphor as well as mechanism. This is where progression couples with expression. Alice’s changing size is both a rule for solving the puzzle and an expression of her unstable relationship to power, identity, and the world around her.
The Entrant discovers what the world permits. The Dreamer discovers what the world’s rules express.

Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland. Illustrated by Gwynedd M. Hudson, 1922 edition.
Surrealism and Dreams
Surrealism was an art movement of the early 20th century. It used dreamlike imagery, unexpected juxtapositions, and illogic to give form to unconscious thoughts, desires, and fears. This transformation of inner experience into visible objects and spaces offers a useful guide to how the Dreamer role can work.

The Burning Giraffe (1937) by Salvador Dalí.
Dream Logic
The Dreamer engages logic — but it is dream logic, cleanly manifested in an early scene in Inception. When Cobb invites Ariadne into a shared dream, she discovers that the space responds to intention: streets fold upward, bridges materialize, and physics bends around the architect’s will.

In a Dreamer game, the first state of L.O.P. — legibility — becomes central to the experience. The rules and relationships of the world are not immediately intuitive. The player discovers them by acting within them, learning to reason as the world responds.

Maquette
Early in Maquette (2021), between narrative scenes, the player stands inside a dome; at its center sits a miniature model of that same space. When a small block is lifted within the model, its massive counterpart moves in the surrounding world. By manipulating the miniature, the player reconfigures the surrounding world and discovers its recursive logic through the response.

The player’s search for passage unfolds across two alternating challenges: configuring the dollhouse-sized architecture, and then platforming through its full-scale counterpart. As the player shifts between these scales, their sense of power and position shifts as well. This structure is not just a puzzle — it becomes surreal language for expressing the emotional stakes of the narrative. Small gestures produce enormous consequences, and meaning emerges through that recursive relationship.
Papo & Yo
Papo & Yo (2012) is the definitive Dreamer project. At a mechanical level, it plays like a standard Entrant game: a boy working through platforming puzzles.

But, crucially, the game is a metaphor for living with an alcoholic parent.

The Monster represents the father. He is gentle and affectionate until he consumes frogs (alcohol), at which point he becomes violent and destructive.
The Puzzles reflect the child’s attempt to control what he can — rearranging spaces and creating pathways forward within a world that remains fundamentally unstable.
The Girl emerges from his imagination. She represents a guiding presence — a way of moving forward, creating distance, and imagining a life beyond the situation.

The mechanics are metaphors. Playing the child of an alcoholic, the player manages the Monster, rearranges spaces, and creates paths forward. Discovery and control unfold together: the player learns the world’s logic while acting within it, and those actions express the attempt to accommodate and ultimately fix the situation. The player eventually confronts the impossibility of doing so. This is what separates The Dreamer from The Entrant: the player still solves puzzles, but those solutions also enact the story’s meaning.
Dreams and Play
Satoshi Kon’s animated film, Paprika, offers a clear image of dreams as living enigmas. Dreams leak into the waking world, culminating in an absurd parade of surreal objects — dancing appliances, walking furniture, and twisting toys — marching through the city.

This is a character’s subconscious made manifest. A Dreamer game can work similarly, turning a character’s inner life into spaces, objects, and rules the player acts upon.
The Dreamer Among the Other Roles
The four roles place discovery and control in different relationships:

The Investigator reconstructs: What happened?
The Traveler witnesses: What is this experience?
The Entrant demonstrates: How does this world work?
The Dreamer enacts: What does this world express?

The Dreamer presents play on two registers: the player solves a mechanical problem while the same actions carry thematic significance. The player may not recognize the metaphor, but they have performed it.

PBOH/Design/Storytelling/index.title: Situated Player Roles
PBOH/Design/Storytelling/index.content:
What They Are For
This framework responds to a challenge every game design course inevitably faces: our initial ideas are too large to build, especially when they involve storytelling.
What It Is
The Situated Player Roles form a game design framework for approaching narrative and worldbuilding through what the player can and cannot do in the world. Inspired by Brian Upton’s Situational Game Design, the framework comprises four roles.
The Four Roles
Two dynamics organize the four roles: discovery and control. Discovery means attending closely to what the world presents by looking, reading, listening, and moving through it. Control means acting upon the world’s state by testing, manipulating, and configuring its systems. Every role involves both dynamics, but places different activities in the foreground. In the Investigator and Traveler, the player’s meaningful mechanics, time, and attention are devoted primarily to discovery. In the Entrant and Dreamer, they are devoted primarily to control. In the first two roles, control enables discovery; in the latter two, discovery enables control.

The Investigator (“What happened?”) — The Investigator reconstructs the story by discovering and engaging evidence — notes, objects, recordings, and NPCs.
The Traveler (“What is this experience?”) — The Traveler discovers meaning by moving through the world, often a labyrinth. Story emerges in real time by exploring a world, shaped by the player’s point of view and the simple act of being there.
The Entrant (“How does this world work?”) — The Entrant is a puzzle solver — learning the logic of the world in order to open blocked passages.
The Dreamer (“What does this world express?”) — The Dreamer begins in the same situation as the Entrant. But here, the structures are dreamlike — actions function as both mechanics and metaphor.

Used Together
A given game may focus on one role or transition players among all four. In every case, the Situated Player Roles treat narrative as something experienced through player verbs. In fact, seen moment to moment, they become stages of player engagement — modes of attention and action that the player shifts among within a natural gameplay loop: the Investigator studies the situation, the Traveler explores it, the Entrant solves it, and the Dreamer enacts its meaning.
The Ambition
This framework does not encompass all approaches and possibilities for narrative game design.
It provides a particular starting point.

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.title: Awkward Exposition
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.content:
Exposition becomes awkward when the world stops moving so it can explain itself — the cutscene, the text scroll, the block of lore. The opposite instinct is embracing Catalysts of Speculation: a designed gap that encourages the player to imagine.
Graceful, Diegetic Options
Ways to deliver exposition that keep the player inside the world:

Environmental storytelling — let the scene carry the history: a barricaded door, a skeleton still clutching its key, a room arranged by whoever lived in it (Gone Home).
Object and item descriptions — lore tucked into the things the player picks up and reads at their own pace (Elden Ring).
Diegetic documents and signage — letters, notes, posters, and screens read in-world (Obra Dinn, Papers, Please).
In-game codex — an optional, player-paced archive of lore reached through a menu, graceful because it’s opt-in— an entry that implies more than it answers (Dark Souls item descriptions) is a catalyst of speculation, rather than a lore-dump.
Audio logs and recordings — voices left behind (BioShock).

Related

Lore as a Trap
Catalysts of Speculation
Teaching the Rules of the World

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.title: Catalysts of Speculation
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.content:
Wolf’s term (p.60) — what the designer leaves untold or unrealized so that the audience imagines it. It is a deliberate withholding that generates an imaginative experience.
Note: this appears to be his own term; not found in wider use apparently.
The Gap
A catalyst of speculation creates a gap — in the story, the situation, or the mechanics. That gap generates anticipation and motivates the player to seek closure — what Gestalt psychology calls the law of closure: the mind completes an incomplete figure on its own. We fill in the gap.
The Zone of Maximum Joy
For players and audiences, the place of maximum joy — the zone in which creators play — is when people believe they can reach closure but don’t feel certainty (Will Storr, The Science of Storytelling).
That uncertainty is pleasant for one of three reasons:

anticipating that the answers are forthcoming;
imagining what is not shown;
or the ambiguity itself is pleasing — closure isn’t wanted or sought.

Two Responses to a Gap
When a catalyst opens a gap, the player can respond in two ways:

Practice closure — the gap generates anticipation, and the player (or reader) fills it in.
Tolerate the gap — the player accepts the gap, perhaps enjoying the lack of closure.

Stories are loops of unknowns preceeding answers. Anticipation is the experience of waiting for the answer. A catalyst of speculation describes a gap we fill in — or one we let stand.
Examples
Jaws — a gap with intent. We barely see the shark; the surface of the water is the boundary, and everything beneath it is withheld. (Practice closure — beneath the water.)

Alien — no origin myth, no backstory, no lore. The derelict ship and its cargo are never explained. (Tolerate the gap.)

Inside — no named institutions, no stated institutional goals. The world withholds the why of everything you flee. (Tolerate the gap.)

Elden Ring — lore exists, but only as fragments. NPCs contradict each other, and the game never confirms a canonical truth. (Tolerate the gap.)

Journey — no explicit objectives and little communication, yet the mountain on the horizon pulls you forward. (Practice closure.)

Two more, told entirely through evidence:

Outer Wilds — the entire game is forensic reconstruction of a dead civilization. Nothing is told to you upfront. The world existed before you arrived and will exist after you’re gone; you’re just reading its traces. (Practice closure.)
Return of the Obra Dinn — you reconstruct what happened to a ship’s crew entirely from frozen moments. The world is implied through evidence, never explained. The gaps are the game. (Practice closure.)

The Pragmatic Case
A catalyst of speculation is effective — and it is also pragmatic. What you imply, you don’t have to build. A gap costs nothing to model, animate, or explain, yet the player’s imagination fills it more richly than any asset might. This is why withholding pairs so naturally with a Bounded World: completeness is a matter of degree, and the unbuilt edges are where speculation does its work.
The PKD Connection
Philip K. Dick: “Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn’t go away.”  Reading - Philip K Dick.
Related

Completeness
Lore as a Trap
Awkward Exposition
Situated Player Roles
Reading - Philip K Dick
Mark Wolf

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.title: Lore as a Trap
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Exposition-and.content:
Lore and backstory are worldbuilding skills that are likely out of scale of the student.  Tolkien needed backstory because he was building a mythology spanning thousands of years, therefore his books took years to write.
In games, the instinct to write lore is a distracton from the essential question: what does the player experience?
Lore-dumping
Defined as delivering world backstory, history, or mythology in an undramatized block — exposition, cutscenes, text walls — rather than letting information emerge through experience. Lore-dumping is when the world stops moving so it can explain itself; it conflicts with the aspirations of the Catalysts of Speculation.
The Provocation
Lore is worldbuilding that failed to manifest through situations. If it’s worthwhile, put it in the playable experience.
Concerning projects of enormous scale, Peter Jackson said the hardest part of Lord of the Rings was backstory - avoiding awkward flashbacks.
The Better Question
Not: what is the history of this world?
But: what can be communicated from inside of it (briefly)?
History and depth can be implied through details — a texture, a sound, even a sign in a language you can’t read — without manifesting them comprehensively.
Games That Imply History Without Explaining It

What Remains of Edith Finch — generations of family history felt through a single house
Return of the Obra Dinn — an entire ship’s history reconstructed from physical evidence alone - this is the core play experience
Firewatch — the Wyoming wilderness feels ancient and layered through environmental design

Related

Transmedia

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Foundations/La.content:
What are you focusing on, as a designer, when you craft your labyrinth?
Do you want the labyrinth’s situations to primarily express meaning, or instead provide the player comprelling choices?
Are they immersed like in most 3D mazes, or looking down, seeing a larger section of the world.
Despite these qualities being set up on linear axes, none of the 4 principles are mutually exclusive.

Worldbuilding - Definition and Scope

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Foundations/St.title: Starting Points for World Creation
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Foundations/St.content:
Every worldbuilding endeavor begins somewhere. Three common entry points:

Story-first — you have a narrative and build the world to support it
Systems-first — you have rules or mechanics and discover the world they imply
World-first — you have a place, and narrative or systems emerge from inhabiting it

Or framed by intent:

Polemic — the world is an argument
Theme — the world is an exploration of an idea
Experience — the world is something you want the player to feel

Situational Game Design
Situational Game Design is a useful influence here, particularly on student-scale projects — the idea that games are designed around a specific player situation.
Related

Worldbuilding - Definition and Scope
Situated Player Roles

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Foundations/Wo.title: Worldbuilding - Definition and Scope
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Foundations/Wo.content:
Wolf (p.17): fictional worlds - we understand them by comparison to reality — the real world is always our starting point, even for the most alien settings.
Zaidi (2019): worlds “provide detailed contextual rule sets that develop a larger reality that extends beyond a single story.” The world is a system; the story runs on top of it.
According to Mark Wolf, worldbuilding constructs a fictional world on three core properties:

Invention — deliberate departure from the primary (real) world
Completeness (a matter of degree) — no world is fully complete, but ancillary detail makes it feel inhabited
Consistency — the world doesn’t contradict itself

Together these earn the world’s plausibility — the belief it asks of the player. Completeness is never total, and those deliberate gaps are what invite the player’s speculation.
Marie-Laure Ryan’s three-part test maps onto the same ground from the player’s side: connected objects (an interrelated network of characters, props, and locations — Wolf’s completeness and structure), a habitable environment (an ecology, physics, or social order that lets inhabitants live and act — consistency made livable), and an intelligible totality (the world reads as a coherent whole — consistency and invention working together).
Worldbuilding ≠ Storytelling
Traditional storytelling values narrative economy — writers include only what advances the story. Worldbuilding does not. Digressions, apparently unnecessary details, and dense data can all be great for expressing a world (Wolf p.29). The detail that goes nowhere in the plot may still do essential work in making the place feel real.
