PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture---Buil.title: Lecture: Building Imaginary Worlds
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture---Buil.content:
This page covers the core vocabulary from Mark Wolf’s Building Imaginary Worlds — a strong reference for worldbuilding terms.


(Spirited Away, 2001 — a world with new logic)
Chihiro’s point-of-view provides a straightforward vehicle for us learn about the world; she is doing so with us. Often, she is as surprised as us.  But sometimes differently - when and how?

Worlds Next to Worlds
Wolf (p.17) says that fictional worlds don’t exist inside our world. They exist in comparison.
The practical consequence: we bring everything we know about the real world with us when we enter a fiction. For example, The Planiverse has seasons, gravity, hunger.
Middle-earth has weather, fatigue, economics.
Our question is, what do they add, subtract, and change?

Definitions
J.R.R. Tolkien’s Groundwork:  Reading - On Fairy-Stories (Tolkien)
→ Worldbuilding - Definition and Scope

According to Wolf, worldbuilding is the process of constructing a fictional world with an interest in:





























Consistency and Internal Logicthe world doesn’t contradict itselfCompletenessno world can be fully complete, but it can feel inhabitedSpeculationthe builder imagines beyond what’s shownInventiondeliberate departure from the primary (real) worldPlausibilitythe world earns belief — a product of the other four

Consistency and Internal Logic
→ Consistency and Internal Logic
Wolf (p.43): a world does not have to be realistic, but it can be consistent.

Baba Is You (2019): the rules of the world are literally written on screen as movable word tiles. Rewrite them, and the world’s rules change.

Completeness
→ Completeness
Wolf (p.38–39): Completeness “refers to the degree to which the world contains explanations and details covering all the various aspects of its characters’ experiences, as well as background details which together suggest a feasible, practical world”.
Ancillary details help believability.

Cyberpunk 2077 (2020) billboards advertise corporations, products, and political slogans that don’t impact the main story.

Elden Ring (2022) reveals the history of the Shattering through item descriptions and environmental storytelling.

Firewatch (2016): the ranger’s backstory unfolds at the beginning.  www.youtube.com/watch

In Middle-earth: the old ruins, the faded maps, the languages with their own grammatical history — these are signals that something happened, long before the story began.

Catalysts of Speculation
→ Catalysts of Speculation
Wolf (p.60): Catalysts of Speculation — what the writer leaves untold, in order to imply.
This is designed ambiguity — a gap that invites the audience to lean in and imagine, or theorize.

2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) — the monolith.

Outer Wilds (2019): the Nomai ruins. What happened to them? In this case the game has an answer — but withholds it long enough that speculation drives exploration.
The end of “The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas” lets us ponder.

Invention (Four Types)
→ Wolf’s Taxonomy of Invention
Wolf (p.34): Invention is the degree to which a world departs from primary world assumptions.  (The “primary world” is the one we live in).
Nominal Invention
Real-world things renamed. The concept works exactly like its real-world equivalent — it’s just called something different.
Star Wars (1977) uses credits instead of money; and parsecs instead of light-years.
In Middle-earth: pipeweed (tobacco), lembas (travel bread), mithril (an ultra-light silver-like metal), mathoms (useless keepsakes you can’t bring yourself to throw away).

(Pipeweed — tobacco by another name.)
The novel Reading - Dark Eden (Beckett) English has changed over five generations of a shipwrecked family.
Cultural Invention
→ Cultural Invention
Social structures, norms, and institutions changed.
In The Planiverse, the 2D creatures have customs for passing one another.
“The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas” (1973)  — Le Guin strips story and context away to examine a single social arrangement: a utopia built on the suffering of one child.
Disco Elysium (2019) comments on (real) history by depicting with a different political configuration.
Natural Invention
→ Nature and Invented Physics
Physics, biology, and ecology changed.

(Arrakis — an entire culture follows from one ecological fact: close to no water)
Arrakis (Dune, 1965): no surface water, sandworms, spice that enables space travel — culture, religion, economics, and body all follow from them.
Outer Wilds (2019): the sun goes supernova every 22 minutes. That single natural law generates the entire game.
In Middle-earth: Dragons, Ents, Balrogs.

(Treebeard —  implies a second biology)
Ontological Invention
The fundamental nature of reality changed.
Annihilation (2018): the rules of identity and biology don’t hold inside Area X.  www.youtube.com/watch

Everything (2017): all matter is conscious and you can play the role of anything.

[[Reading - The Planiverse (Dewdney)|The Planiverse]] (1984): a 2D world — all physics, biology, and architecture follow from having only two spatial dimensions.

In Middle-earth: Magic might be the most common ontological invention in all of fiction.


Wolf’s Eight Elements of Worlds
→ World Structure - Wolf’s Eight Elements
Three foundational structures — the architecture that holds everything else





















Space (Maps)Physical layout: maps, geography, distances, scaleTimelinesHistory, era, how the world ages and changesGeneologiesThe beings who inhabit and act within the world
Five content elements — what fills the world and gives it meaning:





























NatureEcology, physics, biology — the non-human systemsCultureSocial structures, norms, institutions, customsLanguageConstructed languages or naming conventions that imply a systemMythologyCreation stories, religion, legends — what the world tells about itselfPhilosophyWhat the world believes about existence, mortality, good, evil, free will

Space (Maps)

(Tolkien’s original hand-drawn Middle-earth map — he drew it first)
“Maps relate a series of locations to each other, visually unifying them into a world.”
The Middle-earth map is arguably the most famous fantasy map ever made. Tolkien drew it before he wrote the books, using it.

Timeline

World of Warcraft Chronicle Volume 1 (2016) documents the creation of the universe by the Titans, the ordering of Azeroth, the corruption of the Old Gods, the War of the Ancients, and the Great Sundering — all of it unfolding billions of in-world years before a player ever logs in.

Genealogies

Game of Thrones (2011) makes genealogy structural. The family tree is a political map.
“Genealogies relate characters to one another, giving them a context within larger frameworks which are familial, ancestral, social, institutional, and historical. They include such things as family tree charts connecting ancestors and descendants, kinship diagrams of lineal and collateral kin, lineages of rulers and their heirs, and hereditary systems which pass on knowledge, experience, titles, and property down from one generation to another.”

Nature
→ Nature and Invented Physics

“Nature deals with the materiality of a world, its physical, chemical, geological, and biological structures and the ecosystems connecting them.”
Arrakis (Dune, 1965):  Water scarcity shapes culture, religion, economy, and body.

Culture
→ Cultural Invention

Stilgar, leader of the Fremen, spits on the table in front of Duke Leto.  On Arrakis, where water is the most precious substance in the world, offering the moisture of your own body is the highest sign of respect.
“Culture links nature to history and is usually central to the unique situation that provides a story’s conflict; and an invented culture can be more specifically tailored to the author’s needs and does not come with the baggage of an existing culture. By providing a worldview that shapes the natural world’s resources into such things as agriculture, architecture, clothing, vehicles, and artifacts, which in turn inform customs, traditions, language, and mythologies, culture grounds and connects the various productions of a people into a (hopefully) coherent structure through which characters see the secondary world”.

Language

“Many imaginary worlds use constructed languages along with their invented cultures and peoples”.
Tolkien was a professional philologist — a scholar of languages and their histories.

Mythology

Elden Ring (2022) — The Erdtree stands at the center of the Lands Between — a vast, golden, impossibly ancient tree that the game’s entire civilization worships.
“Mythologies structure secondary worlds by giving them a history and context for events, through legends and stories of origins that provide backstories for the current events and settings of a world. They often reveal how characters and ongoing problems came to be, so that story events seem more meaningful and perhaps even the completion of a long character arc or the resolution of an age-old conflict. Mythologies, then, provide historical depth, explanations, and purpose to the events of a world”.

Philosophy

Disco Elysium (2019): explicit political philosophy; the world is a debate about ideologies and what they cost.

The World Is Not A Story, But It Can Facilitate One
→ Completeness
Traditional storytelling values narrative economy — every detail earns its place. Anton Chekhov put it this way:

“If in the first act you have hung a pistol on the wall, then in the following one it should be fired.”

But…
“Worldbuilding doesn’t necessitate narrative economy”.  (p.29)

(Tolkien’s appendices — hundreds of pages of history LOTR never references)
Middle-earth existed as a mythology for decades before The Hobbit. Tolkien’s appendices, the Silmarillion, the Unfinished Tales — most readers don’t read them.
Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018) runs 60+ hours. Most of it has nothing to do with Arthur’s story. NPCs live on schedules. Towns have their own histories. The open world implies a life that goes on whether or not the camera is pointing at it.


Inventions (Wolf p.35)

























TypeWhat it coversNominalNew names for real things (credits instead of dollars)CulturalCustoms, technology, institutions, objects, ideologiesNaturalNew creatures, plants, landmasses (hobbits, sandworms)OntologicalLaws of physics, space, time — deepest level of change
World Elements (Wolf p.154–155)


















































#ElementWhat it covers1SpacePhysical/geographic extent of the world2TimeHistory, present moment, temporal logic3CharactersInhabitants who give the world agency and perspective4NatureLandscape, climate, flora, fauna, physics5CultureCustoms, technology, institutions, objects6LanguageLanguages, dialects, naming conventions7MythologyBelief systems, cosmology, religion, founding stories8PhilosophyUnderlying values; what the world thinks is true
Page References






































































ConceptPageNotePossible worlds framework17Fictional worlds live next to the real world in our mindsRyan’s world definition19Connected objects, habitable environment, intelligible totalityNarrative economy vs. worldbuilding29Worldbuilding doesn’t necessitate narrative economyInvention defined34Degree to which primary world assumptions are changedFour types of invention35Nominal, Cultural, Natural, OntologicalCommon reused inventions37Elves, clones, laser guns, antigravityCompleteness38–39A degree; unnecessary details help believabilityCatalysts of speculation60What you leave untold — Wolf’s own termThree foundational structures154Space, time, charactersFive content elements155Nature, culture, language, mythology, philosophyNarrative defined198–199Causal chain; threads; braidsBackstory202Pre-story narrative
Wolf covers transmedia and AAA scale worldbuilding in later chapters — how games adapt movies, and how large productions approach world design as an explicit discipline.

See also: Worldbuilding - Definition and Scope · Consistency and Internal Logic · Completeness · Catalysts of Speculation · Wolf’s Taxonomy of Invention

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture---Situ.filePath: PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture - Situational Game Design for Bounded Worlds.md
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture---Situ.title: Lecture: Situational Game Design for Bounded Worlds
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Lecture---Situ.content:
This page summarizes the first two chapters of Brian Upton’s Situational Game Design (2017) for the sake of building Bounded Worlds.  All page citations refer to that book.

”A situation is an interval of play that contains a choice.” (p.11)

What Is Situational Game Design?
Most approaches to game design are transactional. They treat games as self-contained systems that stand apart from the player.
Situational game design is different.

“It’s a player-centric approach to design rather than a game-centric one.” (p.5)

Some situations invite interaction. Others invite anticipation, interpretation, or introspection. All of these ways to play contribute to the overall texture of the experience.

“The nexus of play lies not in the interface between the player and the game, but inside the player’s mind.  Games are not playful in and of themselves. ” (p.6)



                  
                  Hold On 
                  
                

Upton’s take precedes today’s version of the A.I. topic “am I going to be replaced?” His approach keeps the player — the human — at the nexus of the system.  This reminds us how games as art ponder culture - does this game (my life) need to be transactional?



Games Are More Than Interaction
Yes, games are interactive. But to often game design theory treats interactivity as the whole show — how to structure mechanics, create agency, provide feedback, deliver accomplishment.
Many games feel playful even when we aren’t interacting with them.

“A sustained feeling of playfulness spans the intervals between our interactions. Making moves is an essential part of the experience of playing chess, but if we want to understand how it feels to play chess, we also need to understand how play unfolds when we’re not moving.” (p.1)

Chess — between moves, you’re reading the board, imagining futures, feeling pressure. That’s play.

P.T. — the interactivity is limited. What makes it work is the tension between actions.

Peter: People want their field to be special. Game design folks often privlidge what qualities aren’t in other media — like interaction. But if we acknowledge that control doesn’t have to be at the center of our model, what creative opportunites open up?
Like other forms of art, games encourage us to ponder and process culture.  And so, is there more to computing than efficiency and power?


Film cuts as analogy
We can draw an analogy between interactivity in games and the cut in cinema.

“The cut is a thing that a film can do, but it’s not a thing that a film must do. A film doesn’t cease being a film during a long continuous shot.” (p.2)

More cuts doesn’t mean a better film. More interaction doesn’t mean a better game.

“Interactivity is a thing that a game can do, but it’s not a thing that a game must do. A game doesn’t cease being a game if it contains long stretches where the player doesn’t interact.  = Sometimes, the most playful thing a game can do is hold still.” (p.2)


The Problem with Winning
There’s another assumption: games are about winning. Our moves are always directed toward satisfying a win condition.

Peter:  True, games can be “play plus winning”, but that does not define the big picture.


D&D — Players are expected to stay alive, accumulate treasure, level up.  But sometimes players deliberately choose losing moves. A player may throw away a rare spell book because they’re playing an illiterate barbarian. Players pursue intrinsic motivations derived from character, narrative, and situation.

Sometimes, play is performance… Sometimes, play is exploration… Sometimes, play is destruction… Sometimes, play is camaraderie.” (p.4)



Peter: If your Bounded World isn’t about winning, what is the player doing there? What is the experience you’re making?


Making Meaning with Games
The standard way to understand meaning-making is semiotics. Transmission model: speaker encodes, listener decodes. This works well for books and movies.
Like metaphor.
Semiotics is the study of how meaning gets made and transmitted. The core model is simple: a creator encodes meaning into a work, and the audience decodes it. The meaning travels from one to the other through a sign system — language, image, music, editing, all of it.
Cinema is a sign system. The director controls what you see, when you see it, what you hear, how long a shot lingers, where the cut falls.
La Maison en Petits Cubes encodes an entire life — through image and score. Every viewer decodes the same thing: grief, delivered.


“But the standard semiotic model breaks down when we get at the heart of how meaning-making operates in games. Much of the meaning that we take away from a game is not a function of the signifiers that it transmits to us, but rather of the things it allows us to do. Performance is where much of the meaning of a game lies.” (p.7)

Here meaning is constructed, not transmitted.

Peter: So “playing pretend” is an example?

In Journey, meaning-making is not explainable through the standard semiotic model because its meaning doesn’t arise from a transmission of signifiers.


Situations and Constraints

“A situation is an interval of play that contains a choice.” (p.11)

A turn in Monopoly, a platform in Super Mario Bros., entering a door in DOOM, a moment in Tetris — all of these are situations.


“We can conceptualize any play experience as a chain of situations. Within each situation we have a choice of moves, and the move we choose determines our next situation.” (p.11)


Peter:  Choosing to run towards a distant tree is a choice, just as valuable (expressive) as choosing to use a weapon against a boss.

Constraints
Situations are structured by constraints. The constraints determine which moves we’re allowed to make and therefore what choices the situation offers.

“The most obvious type of constraint is a rule.” (p.12)

But rules aren’t the only type of constraint.

“We can be constrained by level layout, or by enemy behavior, or by real-world physics, or by social convention, or by our sense of performing a role, or by our own strategies.” (p.13)


→ The Entrant: A Response to Situational Game Design

The Entrant is part of a larger framework.  The Entrant confronts a threshold — a constraint that blocks passage. The player reads the space (Legibility), imagines how to proceed (Opportunity) , before executing the plan (Performance).

→ Bounded Worlds
Your Bounded World is a constraint structure. The three types — Finite, Closed, and Threshold — these are constraint designs. How does the player encounter the limits?
Let’s look at Balance, Dr Langeskov, and  The Matrix.  Let’s move backwards through them.

Game as Designed, Experienced, Understood
Different constraints are enforced in different ways. Sometimes we enforce them on ourselves; other times they’re imposed upon us.
We avoid colliding with walls in a first-person shooter. We avoid picking up the ball in a soccer match. We don’t steal money in Monopoly.

Peter: We often think the difference between board games and video games is audiovisual. But most important is external vs. internal constraints. You can peek in solitaire but you can’t in Hearthstone.

Three different aspects of any game:

Game as Designed — the system of external constraints created by the designer. Written rules, intended physicality, programmatic embodiment.
Game as Experienced — how the designer’s intent manifests within a particular play session. The chain of situations it evokes.
Game as Understood — our personal grasp of the game. Our internal mental representation of its rules and physicality, our grasp of its social context, and our sense of what strategies it requires.


“There are always situations that the rules permit that don’t arise when the game is played, and there are always situations that arise when the game is played that the designer never anticipated.” (p.17)

Exploits — when the gap between our understanding and the game’s programming becomes noticeable. An exploit is a hole in our understanding, not in the game’s code. The game always does exactly what its code says it should.

Pre-existing Constraints
We bring our own pre-existing internal constraints. Some come from our understanding of the real world, others from other games.

Peter: Much of the value of a class - like this one - derives from the collection of constraints on you: both enforced and not enforced.

We avoid hills in video games even when the game doesn’t penalize climbing. We follow paths. We resist stepping into water. These soft pathing constraints affect the situations we encounter as we play.

“A genre is a collection of constraints that players can take as a given.” (p.20)

If you’re playing a horror game, you’ll move differently than if you believe you’re playing a first-person shooter. You’ll be more cautious. You’ll pay more attention. Part of what makes a horror game scary is our knowledge that it’s supposed to be scary.

Peter:  In your Bounded World, does the player constrain themselves?


Source: Chapters 1–2, Situational Game Design
See also: Situated Player Role 3 - The Entrant · Bounded Worlds

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.title: Meeting the World
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.content:
Let us focus on brief moments within a situation, steps within “the interval of play” articulated in Situational Game Design for Bounded Worlds.

“A situation is an interval of play that contains a choice.” (p.11)

We are interested in both the moment before and after entry.   Ponder your player’s experience of legibility when it comes to your Bounded World boundary - the experience of playing and the emotions it affords.
What that player attention achieves is intrinsic: beauty, awe, curiosity, dread, excitement — play without winning.
In particular, constraints are expressive, in this case, boundaries.
Topics

Bounded Worlds
Legibility
Entry/transitions
Situations
Inventions

Crimson Desert
The map (lower-left) shows the goal, quiet and small.
The constraint demands awe; we see and feel the cliff as a boundary.


Piranesi
We begin the novel with time, tides, and a touchstone.
“When the Moon rose in the Third Northern Hall I went to the Ninth Vestibule
ENTRY FOR THE FIRST DAY OF THE FIFTH MONTH IN THE YEAR THE ALBATROSS CAME TO THE SOUTH-WESTERN HALLS
When the Moon rose in the Third Northern Hall I went to the Ninth Vestibule to witness the joining of three Tides. This is something that happens only once every eight years.
The Ninth Vestibule is remarkable for the three great Staircases it contains. Its Walls are lined with marble Statues, hundreds upon hundreds of them, Tier upon Tier, rising into the distant heights”.

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.title: Teaching the Rules of the World
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.content:
A primary design challenge for video game designers is teaching the player how to play.  This is teaching the rules of the world.
Two approaches:


Explicit tutorial — the world pauses to explain itself.  This can feel artificial, but might be needed when the rules are intricate. Soul (2020) does this in film: when Joe arrives in the Great Before, the Jerrys explain how souls work before the story can continue.  (Workable at Pixar’s scale; likely a bad model for student projects).
www.youtube.com/watch


Teaching through play — the early levels function as the tutorial. The world’s rules emerge through low-stakes encounters before the player faces real consequences. Portal is a clear example: early chambers each introduce one mechanic, invites you to learn through play, before you venture to the next one.  Baba Is You takes this further: the rules are literally objects in the world.


This aethetic aspiration comports with all genres.  Any early section — whether labeled a tutorial or not — teaches you the world’s core systems before it moves on with complexity.
Related

Nature and Invented Physics
Consistency and Internal Logic
Lore as a Trap
Portal
Baba Is You

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.title: World Responsiveness
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.content:
A world’s responsiveness is what makes a space feel inhabited and exciting — it has precence, behavior, and consequence.
Let us craft our world’s responsiveness with a pragmatic thread: a set of Unreal Tutorials for beginners.
To say a world is responsive is to say it reacts to the player’s presence. A pressure plate opens a door. A light turns on when you enter a room. A sound plays when you step on the wrong tile. These are simple, but they establish: the world knows you’re there.
More complex forms:

Events triggered by what the player has done (not just where they are)
World state that persists and changes over time
Inhabitants who respond to the player’s cumulative decisions, not just their current position

The Haunted House as Model
The haunted house is a good framing because it makes explicit: the world is performing for the player. Lights, doors, NPCs, and sounds are the world’s expressive vocabulary.
Related

Consistency and Internal Logic
Situated Player Roles

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.title: The Experience
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/The-Experience.content:
The designed moments where a player meets and inhabits the world — crossing in, the world answering back, and learning its rules through play rather than explanation.

Meeting the World — how and where the player starts; the entry as a designed moment
World Responsiveness — how the world reacts to the player
Teaching the Rules of the World — teaching invented rules through play, not tutorialization

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Vocabulary/Com.title: Completeness
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Vocabulary/Com.content:
Mark Wolf (p.38–39): completeness is a degree.  Every world has gaps. The question is how those gaps are handled.
In worldbuilding, unnecessary details might help believability, unlike traditional storytelling (where every detail earns its place by advancing the plot). In worldbuilding a detail that goes nowhere narratively can still make the place feel inhabited.

PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Vocabulary/Con.title: Consistency and Internal Logic
PBOH/Design/Worldbuilding/Vocabulary/Con.content:
Mark Wolf (p.43): consistency is the degree to which world details are plausible, feasible, and without contradiction.
Rather than strive to make a world realistic (as we don’t know what that means), aim to make it consistent. The rules can be surprising, even impossible, but once established, they work moving forward.
The Secret World of Arrietty
We deduce scale quite easily.

9:24 (a trek)
25:35 (compare her size to the roly poly)
59:25 (comparison again)
play.hbomax.com/video/watch/01c72e76-910b-43e4-93b2-bcc337b0d93b/086662ec-0ac6-4603-8ceb-a62be62b3d1d

The Road Runner - We Learn
The Road Runner cartoon doesn’t violates its own physics, however absurd the physics are. Wile E. Coyote survives explosions, falls, and being flattened.  The payoff of most of these shorts is the unexpected invention’s reveal.

7:10 — painting a tunnel onto a cliff face
8:30 — skiing on air
14:25 — iconic fall
www.youtube.com/watch


The outcome of each trap is to teach us one of the world’s rules.
His traps leads to surprises (rather than successes). The surprises (a new rule we’re learning) work because the prior rules are established to work as a system.
Cartoonish gravity, speed, specific materials (bombs, meat grinders, labeled boxes of gadgets) — these form a consistent system.


                  
                  Hold On > > A note about narrative vs play: if this were a game, we would try the same worthwhile approaches until we succeed, or at least more than once.  Wile E. Coyote does not retry his ideas. 
                  
                

Operating in a Finite World

La Maison en Petits by Kunio Kato.  The way architecture is metaphor and a vehicles for storytelling is consistent and leverages rather straightforward logic.
His journey downward triggers flashbacks, each futher back in time as he visits deeper chambers of his home.
His impossibly tall home was build over his lifetime, each “story” of the building is a story.
The water rises.  He builds upward, just a little ahead of the water - a metaphor for the inevitable end of his life.
We discover the world with and through him, as he explores.
www.youtube.com/watch
Game Examples

Portal — a pinnacle example of how rule consistency and incrementally teaching the player couple.  For example, when the ability to place the second portal (orange) emerges, the logic otherwise does not change.
Baba Is You — rules are literally word blocks. When you reconfigure them, core gameplay changes.
Inscryption — the card game’s internal rules are consistent even as the meta-layer shifts around them.
Rain World — the ecosystem runs on its own schedule regardless of the player’s impact.

Related
