PBOH/Design/_References/Game---PT.title: Game - PT
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---PT.content:
Developer: Kojima Productions | Year: 2014 | Platform: PS4 (delisted)
P.T. (Playable Teaser) is a first-person horror demo created as a teaser for a cancelled Silent Hill collaboration between Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro. The player walks through an L-shaped hallway that loops endlessly, each pass revealing new details.
www.youtube.com/watch

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Papers-Pl.title: Game - Papers Please
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Papers-Pl.content:
Developer: Lucas Pope | Year: 2013 | Platform: PC, mobile, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A border-checkpoint simulator set in the fictional communist state of Arstotzka. The player is an immigration inspector processing travelers one at a time — comparing passports, work permits, entry tickets, and ID cards against an ever-changing rulebook. Approve or deny. Catch a forged seal or expired date and you’re paid; miss one and your family doesn’t eat. The bureaucratic procedure is the gameplay, and moral pressure builds as the rules grow more punitive.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Papo-and-.title: Game - Papo and Yo
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Papo-and-.content:
Developer: Minority | Year: 2012 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A puzzle-platformer set in a favela. Your companion is a giant monster. The monster is helpful when calm, but when he eats frogs, he becomes violent and dangerous. The game is autobiographical allegory: the developer’s father was an alcoholic.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Picnic-Pa.title: Game - Picnic Pals
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Picnic-Pa.content:
Developer: USC student team | Year: 2023 | Platform: PC
A 489 project built around a single puzzle / optimization mechanic with variations developed across a small set of levels. Simple but effective art; enough variety for a handful of levels; smooth progression. A good model of an appropriately-scoped Intermediate project.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Pitfall.title: Game - Pitfall
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Pitfall.content:
Developer: Activision (David Crane) | Year: 1982 | Platform: Atari 2600
A side-scrolling jungle adventure. Pitfall Harry runs through screens of scorpions, snakes, crocodiles, vines, and pits, collecting treasures against a 20-minute timer. Used in 389 as the in-class exercise for writing a macro for a small classic game.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Plug--and.title: Game - Plug & Play
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Plug--and.content:
Developer: Michael Frei & Mario von Rickenbach (Etter Studio / Playables) | Year: 2015 | Platform: PC, mobile
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Steam
What It Is
A 15-minute interactive animation in stark black-and-white: figures with plugs and sockets for heads connect, disconnect, obey and defy a commanding voice, and reach for each other. Based on Frei’s award-winning animated short, it sits deliberately on the line between game and film — minimal forms, absurdist logic, and a surprising amount of feeling about connection and consent. (Same maker as Time Flies and KIDS.)

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Pony-Isla.title: Game - Pony Island
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Pony-Isla.content:
Developer: Daniel Mullins Games | Year: 2016 | Platform: PC
→ Steam
What It Is
A moody puzzle game disguised as a cheerful, broken arcade game. The player begins by trying to play the game presented on screen, then discovers that its menus, errors, code, and apparent machine are all part of the playable world.
Expectation and Payoff
The title, menu, graphics, and first simple actions establish the contract of a crude pony-themed arcade game. Small malfunctions make that contract unstable before the game reveals a second layer behind the interface.
The surprise is not a single unrelated twist. Each failure of the arcade game teaches the player to treat the interface itself as a space to investigate and manipulate. The payoff changes what kind of game the player believes they are playing.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Portal-2.title: Game - Portal 2
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Portal-2.content:
Developer: Valve | Year: 2011 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A first-person puzzle game set in the ruined Aperture Science testing facility. Portal 2 expands the original game’s portal mechanic with new characters, surfaces, gels, and machinery, while the facility itself changes around the player.
Expectation and Payoff
The opening begins with a tiny domestic routine. An automated voice asks the player to look around and return to bed, establishing the room as a stable place and the instructions as the game’s apparent rhythm.
When Wheatley arrives, that same room is torn from its setting and carried through a collapsing facility. The payoff grows directly from the setup: an ordinary room becomes a vehicle, its walls become a thin disguise, and the scale and condition of the world are revealed through its destruction.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Portal.title: Game - Portal
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Portal.content:
Developer: Valve | Year: 2007 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A first-person puzzle game. You have a portal gun that creates linked openings in surfaces. The world is a testing facility. GLaDOS watches.
As the player gains control of the portals, the logic is consistent.

0:20 - trapped
1:05 - portals given
3:09 - gun creates blue portal
13:20 - gun creates orange portal as well
www.youtube.com/watch

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Proteus.title: Game - Proteus
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Proteus.content:
Developer: Ed Key & David Kanaga | Year: 2013 | Platform: PC, PlayStation
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Steam
What It Is
A procedurally generated pastel island with no goals, no text, and no hands — just walking and listening. Every plant, animal, and weather pattern emits its own musical signature, so the soundtrack is your position in the world: chase frogs and the music hops, stand in rain and it shimmers. A season passes when you let it. The purest available example of presence and witnessing as the entire design.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Psychonau.title: Game - Psychonauts
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Psychonau.content:
Developer: Double Fine Productions | Year: 2005 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A third-person platformer. You play Raz, a psychic kid at a summer camp for psychic children. a primary mechanic: enter the minds of NPCs and navigate them as distinct physical worlds. Each mental world is a bounded, self-contained space inside that character’s mind.
Inside Coach Oleander’s mind:  youtu.be/HxtFsjS7-ok

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Rain-Worl.title: Game - Rain World
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Rain-Worl.content:
Developer: Videocult | Year: 2017 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A survival platformer set in a collapsed industrial ecosystem. You play a slugcat — small, slow, and prey. The food chain runs without you. Predators hunt on their own schedule. The world is indifferent to your survival.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Red-Dead-.title: Game - Red Dead Redemption 2
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Red-Dead-.content:
Developer: Rockstar Games | Year: 2018 | Platform: PC, console
What It Is
An open-world western following Arthur Morgan, an outlaw in a gang at the end of the frontier era. The world is built at a scale that dwarfs its story — NPCs live on schedules, towns have their own economies, ecosystems run independently of the player.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Return-of.filePath: PBOH/Design/_References/Game - Return of the Obra Dinn.md
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Return-of.title: Game - Return of the Obra Dinn
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Return-of.content:
Developer: Lucas Pope | Year: 2018 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
An insurance investigation game. You board a ghost ship and reconstruct what happened to its entire crew, one death at a time, using a magical pocket watch that shows frozen moments from the past.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Return-to.title: Game - Return to Zork
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Return-to.content:
Developer: Infocom / Activision | Year: 1993 | Platform: PC (CD-ROM)
A first-person CD-ROM adventure held in high regard as a product of its era. Contains canonical examples of bad mazes — disorienting brute-force corridors with no design intent beyond requiring the player to draw a map. The kind of maze the Lost Woods design tradition is a response to.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Roller-Co.title: Game - Roller Coaster Tycoon
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Roller-Co.content:
Developer: Chris Sawyer | Year: 1999 (the version cited in lecture: 2003 platinum) | Platform: PC
→ Steam
A theme park management sim. New rides and upgrades take in-game time to research and build, and the game reveals a new animation or model when each one unlocks — wait time itself becomes a source of anticipation.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Shadow-of.title: Game - Shadow of the Colossus
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Shadow-of.content:
Developer: Team Ico | Year: 2005 (remake 2018) | Platform: PS2, PS3, PS4
→ PlayStation Store
A third-person action game in which the player must kill sixteen massive creatures to revive a girl. Early colossi feel like ARPG bosses: exciting, satisfying. Over time the satisfaction sours — the colossi aren’t monstrous but majestic, and the player isn’t a hero but a villain. A reference for how mechanical and aesthetic framing can carry a moral argument.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Sherlock-.title: Game - Sherlock Holmes 2021
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Sherlock-.content:
Developer: Frogwares | Year: 2021 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
Sherlock Holmes: Chapter One. A modern open-world detective game continuing the puzzle / mystery lineage that interactive fiction helped establish.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Silly-Mas.title: Game - Silly Masterpiece
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Silly-Mas.content:
Developer: USC student team | Year: 2024 | Platform: PC
A 489 project that leans on programming over art. Simple mechanics require some tricky implementation; the character controller is highly polished. The character itself is crude — but tweening and particle effects bring it to life.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Slash-Bas.title: Game - Slash Bash
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Slash-Bas.content:
Developer: USC student team | Year: 2024 | Platform: PC
A 489 project: a constrained but impressive fighting game. Controller support, heavy post-processing, a training mode — but no networking. Modular content (multiple characters and levels) helps keep scope under control. A reference for scope-discipline in a genre that usually overreaches.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Spec-Ops-.title: Game - Spec Ops The Line
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Spec-Ops-.content:
Developer: Yager | Year: 2012 | Platform: PC, console
A third-person military shooter set in post-disaster Dubai. Presents itself as a middle-of-the-road 2010s shooter; ends as a meditation on player complicity. The revelation reframes the player’s relationship to the violence they’ve enacted — a touchstone for Revelation and Recontextualization and for games that interrogate their own genre.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Stray.title: Game - Stray
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Stray.content:
Developer: BlueTwelve Studio | Year: 2022 | Platform: PC, PlayStation, Xbox
Fame tier: famous
→ Steam
What It Is
A stray cat falls into a sealed, neon-lit underground city populated entirely by robots who have inherited human culture, and works its way back toward the surface with a small drone translator. The whole design flows from the body: you move through a world built for other inhabitants — rooftops, pipes, gaps — as the one creature the architecture wasn’t made for. Bounded world, found companionship, and cat-verbs (knock things off shelves, scratch, curl up) as world-reading tools.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Subnautic.title: Game - Subnautica
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Subnautic.content:
Developer: Unknown Worlds | Year: 2018 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
The reference 3D survival game. Your ship crashes on an alien ocean planet and you’re alone underwater. You gather resources, craft tools, build bases, and manage oxygen, hunger, and thirst while descending into ever-deeper, darker biomes — and slowly uncover what happened to the planet’s vanished inhabitants and why no rescue is coming.
Survival as Worldbuilding
Most survival games are systems first and world second. Subnautica is the opposite — its survival loop is inseparable from its world:

The world’s nature sets the rules. Oxygen, pressure, and light aren’t UI numbers bolted on; they’re the invented nature of an ocean planet, and they dictate how you can move and how deep you dare go. The biome is the difficulty curve.
Descent is the dread. There are almost no weapons. The threat is the world itself — the dark, the depth, the things larger than you that you can only flee. Fear comes from going down, not from combat.
The story is in the water. What happened here — a crashed ship, an alien plague, a long-dead Precursor civilization — is reconstructed from wreckage, data logs, and ruins. Pure environmental storytelling: the world existed before you and withholds most of its answers.

That makes it a strong Investigator (read the wreck for what happened) and Traveler (the ocean is to be moved through and witnessed) example — survival mechanics carrying a genuine world, not just a stat economy.
What to Pull From It For a Survival Project
Before reaching for crafting menus and hunger bars, ask what Subnautica asks: what does this world’s nature force the player to do, and what does the place withhold that pulls them deeper?
Related

Nature and Invented Physics — the world’s nature as the survival ruleset
Catalysts of Speculation — story reconstructed from wreckage and ruins
Game - Rain World — survival where you’re prey in an indifferent ecology (a different flavor)

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Superlimi.title: Game - Superliminal
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Superlimi.content:
Developer: Pillow Castle Games | Year: 2019 | Platform: PC, console
**→ Steam
What It Is
A first-person puzzle game played inside a dream. The central mechanic is forced perspective: pick up an object, move it closer or farther from the camera, and it physically resizes to match its apparent size. A chess piece held against a doorway becomes a chess piece tall enough to climb. Framed as a sleep-therapy program gone strange.
youtu.be/yvzySTxBFIQ

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Tacoma.title: Game - Tacoma
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Tacoma.content:
Developer: The Fullbright Company
→ Steam
Year: 2017
Platform: PC
Fame tier: successful indie
A first-person investigation game set on an abandoned space station. The player reconstructs a crisis by scrubbing through 3D AR recordings of the crew — replaying their movements, conversations, and actions from multiple angles to piece together what went wrong.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Begin.title: Game - The Beginner's Guide
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Begin.content:
Developer: Davey Wreden | Year: 2015 | Platform: PC
→ Steam
A first-person narrative game framed as a guided tour through another (fictional) designer’s body of work. The sense that something is wrong builds slowly through the second half — the player anticipates a change without knowing what shape it will take. A reference for looming-revelation anticipation.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Grave.title: Game - The Graveyard
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Grave.content:
Developer: Tale of Tales | Year: 2008 | Platform: PC, Mac
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Steam
What It Is
You play an elderly woman who walks — slowly, with a cane — down the central path of a graveyard, sits on a bench, and listens to a song. That’s the whole game; the developers call it “an explorable painting.” In the full version, each play carries a chance she dies of natural causes on the bench. From the makers of The Path: presence, mortality, and a single short walk asked to carry everything.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Lante.title: Game - The Lantern
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Lante.content:
Developer: USC student team | Year: 2024 | Platform: PC
A 489 project that started very ambitious and scaled back when the team realized they couldn’t make as much content as planned. The clear aesthetic vision held the whole thing together in the end, but the project would have benefited from focusing on fewer mechanics earlier. A scope-management reference.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Last-.title: Game - The Last of Us
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Last-.content:
Developer: Naughty Dog | Year: 2013 (remake 2022) | Platform: PC, PlayStation
→ Steam
A third-person post-apocalyptic action-adventure. Many of its key-and-door puzzles use environmental fiction: a powered door needs a generator turned on; a high jump needs a dumpster pushed into position. The keys are tools and props, not literal keys.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Path.title: Game - The Path
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Path.content:
Developer: Tale of Tales | Year: 2009 | Platform: PC, Mac
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Wikipedia
What It Is
A retelling of Little Red Riding Hood. You play six sisters in turn; each is told to walk to grandmother’s house and stay on the path. The actual game is what happens when you leave it — each sister meets her own wolf in the forest, a figure shaped to her particular age and identity. The canonical Traveler game: a clear instruction the world is built for you to reconsider, where straying is the meaning.
Playthrough: www.youtube.com/watch

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Pedes.title: Game - The Pedestrian
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Pedes.content:
Developer: Skookum Arts | Year: 2020 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A puzzle platformer where you play as the figure from a pedestrian-crossing sign, hopping between panels of public signage by rearranging them. The world is the visual furniture of city life — restroom icons, fire-exit diagrams, restaurant menus — re-seen as a place you can move through.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Stanl.title: Game - The Stanley Parable
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Stanl.content:
Developer: Galactic Cafe | Year: 2013 (Ultra Deluxe 2022) | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A first-person exploration game in which a narrator describes everything Stanley — you — does, in past tense, as if it’s already written. You can follow the narration or defy it; each branch is a different short ending, and the game keeps acknowledging that it knows you’re playing it. A piece about authorial control, illusion of choice, and what a game is.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Talos.title: Game - The Talos Principle
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Talos.content:
Developer: Croteam (writers Tom Jubert & Jonas Kyratzes) | Year: 2014 | Platform: PC, console
Fame tier: successful indie
→ Steam
What It Is
A robot wakes in sunlit classical ruins where a sky-voice claiming to be God assigns puzzle after puzzle — lasers to route, drones to divert, time to replicate — while terminals scattered through the world needle you with philosophical questions about what you are and whether to obey. The puzzles teach mastery; the world teaches doubt — meaning lives in whether you climb the forbidden tower.
Its variation on keys-and-doors: a single kind of key opens three different kinds of doors. The purple portal visible in the first moments serves as doorway, landmark, and objective — a clean example of Reusing Objects and Spaces.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Unfin.title: Game - The Unfinished Swan
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---The-Unfin.content:
Developer: Giant Sparrow | Year: 2012 | Platform: PS3/PS4, iOS, PC
→ Steam
What It Is
A first-person fairy tale that begins in a completely white world — you throw blobs of black paint to reveal the environment as you go. A boy named Monroe chases an unfinished swan from his late mother’s painting into the unfinished kingdom of an absent king. Each chapter overturns the previous mechanic (paint, then light and shadow, then vines that grow where you spray water, then building blocks).

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Thirty-Fl.title: Game - Thirty Flights of Loving
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Thirty-Fl.content:
Developer: Blendo Games (Brendon Chung) | Year: 2012 | Platform: PC
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Steam
What It Is
A fifteen-minute first-person story about a heist gone wrong, told with jump cuts — the game hard-cuts you between moments mid-stride, out of order, and trusts you to assemble the story from fragments: a wedding, an airport, an orange peeled in slow motion. The first game to seriously import film editing into first-person space. The reference for non-linear storytelling through abrupt, confident scene transitions.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Thomas-Wa.title: Game - Thomas Was Alone
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Thomas-Wa.content:
Developer: Mike Bithell | Year: 2012 | Platform: PC
→ Steam
Thomas Was Alone is a minimalist platformer in which colored rectangles — each with a distinct personality narrated by Danny Wallace — navigate puzzle environments.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Time-Flie.title: Game - Time Flies
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Time-Flie.content:
Developer: Playables (Michael Frei & Raphaël Munoz), published by Panic | Year: 2025 | Platform: PC, Switch, PlayStation
Fame tier: cult-niche
→ Steam
What It Is
You are a fly. Your lifespan matches the life expectancy of the country you set — a few real minutes — and you have a bucket list: learn an instrument, read a book, get rich, make someone smile. Each tiny life is spent bumbling through hand-drawn rooms trying to check items off before you drop. Mortality as a mechanic at its lightest possible touch: the timer is the whole design, and it’s funny until it isn’t. (Same maker as Plug & Play.)

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Up-the-Ri.title: Game - Up the River
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Up-the-Ri.content:
Designer: Erhard Wissner | Publisher: Ravensburger | Year: 1988 | Platform: Tabletop
A family board game in which players race small boats up a river against a tide that pushes everything back. Its procedural rhetoric: boats are meant to reach a destination; persistence beats environment; luck, speed, and sacrifice are rewarded; it’s better to be self-interested than spiteful; only one person can win.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Viewfinde.title: Game - Viewfinder
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Viewfinde.content:
Developer: Sad Owl Studios | Year: 2023 | Platform: PC, PlayStation
Fame tier: successful indie
→ Steam
What It Is
You hold up a photograph — a postcard, a sketch, a child’s drawing — and place it into the world, where it becomes real, walkable geometry that replaces whatever was behind it. Bridges from postcards, doors from sketches, whole rooms cut out of pictures. One reality-bending camera mechanic, taught and escalated with total clarity. The reference for perspective-as-mechanic and for a single impossible rule explored to exhaustion.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---What-Rema.filePath: PBOH/Design/_References/Game - What Remains of Edith Finch.md
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---What-Rema.title: Game - What Remains of Edith Finch
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---What-Rema.content:
Developer: Giant Sparrow | Year: 2017 | Platform: PC, console
→ Steam
What It Is
A walking simulator about a family home. Each room is a complete self-contained story — and a world-within-a-world. You play through the deaths of each family member, each in a completely different visual style and mechanic.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Who's-Lil.title: Game - Who's Lila
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---Who's-Lil.content:
Developer: Garage Heathen | Year: 2022 | Platform: PC
→ Steam
A psychological horror adventure with a distinctive mechanic: the player must manually manipulate the protagonist’s face to mimic appropriate facial expressions during conversations. The recurring face-control beats emphasize how alienated the player character feels — a mechanic carrying narrative weight.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---World-of-.title: Game - World of Warcraft
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---World-of-.content:
Developer: Blizzard Entertainment | Year: 2004 | Platform: PC
→ Wikipedia
What It Is
A massively multiplayer RPG set in Azeroth — a world with dozens of distinct races and factions, each with their own history, architecture, music, and values.
The world is the main character.

PBOH/Design/_References/Game---apartment.title: Game - apartment a separated place
PBOH/Design/_References/Game---apartment.content:
Developer: The Elsewhere Company | Year: 2020 | Platform: PC
→ Steam
What It Is
A short, text-heavy interactive narrative about a breakup. Nick has just been left by Madison after four years; you enter his apartment in the aftermath and move through his memories of the relationship. You also step into neighbors’ apartments — small interactive vignettes, each its own study of love and isolation. There is little to do in the action sense; the game is environmental storytelling and reading, intimate and introspective, built to sit with loss rather than resolve it.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Aesop'.title: Reading - Aesop's Fables (Aesop)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Aesop'.content:
Author: attributed to Aesop · Year: c. 6th century BCE (collected later) · Type: Fables
→ Wikipedia
Summary
A body of short tales, each a few lines long, traditionally credited to Aesop — a storyteller of ancient Greece — though most were gathered by others across the centuries after him. Each fable is a self-contained little story, usually starring animals who talk and act like people, and each ends by making a single point: a moral. They began as spoken stories and were only written down and collected generations later, which is part of why so many unattributed tales ended up under Aesop’s name.
The best-known example is The Boy Who Cried Wolf. A shepherd boy, bored on the hillside, twice tricks the villagers by shouting that a wolf is attacking his flock; they come running, find nothing, and go back annoyed. When a real wolf finally comes and the boy cries out in earnest, no one believes him — and the flock is lost. The moral: a liar is not believed even when he tells the truth.
Relevance to Worldbuilding
Each fable is a compact model of a Finite world — a world complete in a handful of lines, with nothing outside what the story needs. The Boy Who Cried Wolf is the clean example: the world is exactly the pasture, the boy, the sheep, the villagers, and the wolf. There is no wider town, no history, no elsewhere.
Also useful across the Situated Player Roles as a study in economy: how little a world can contain and still say something.
Related

Bounded Worlds
Situated Player Roles

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Alice'.title: Reading - Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (Carroll)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Alice'.content:
Author: Lewis Carroll · Year: 1865 · Type: Novel
→ Wikipedia
Summary
Bored on a riverbank, Alice notices a White Rabbit in a waistcoat checking a pocket watch — and, curious, follows it down the rabbit hole. The fall is long and slow, and by the time it ends she has left the ordinary world entirely: she is in Wonderland, where the rules of waking life no longer apply. What follows is a string of encounters — the “Drink Me” bottle and “Eat Me” cake that shrink and grow her, the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter’s tea party, the Queen of Hearts and her croquet — each governed by a logic that is internally consistent yet absurd. Wonderland is a self-contained world that runs on dream logic; nonsense there is its own kind of sense.
The rabbit hole is the crossing. It is the moment the world changes state — the threshold between the everyday and the other-world — and everything after it belongs to Wonderland’s rules, not ours.
Demonstration
youtu.be/Q93VrYOXSe8
Relevance to Storytelling and Worldbuilding
Two axes meet in Alice, defining it as a primary text for both game storytelling and worldbuilding.
Within the Bounded Worlds framework, Wonderland is a Bounded World.  Passing through a boundary is primary:  the rabbit hole is a designed crossing, a single moment that carries [the player] from one order of reality into another, ushering in a new set of rules. The descent itself — long, disorienting— is the entry that tells the player that they can anticipate learning the inventions of the world.
In terms of storytelling, Alice is the foundation for the Situated Player Role, The Dreamer. Wonderland is dream logic made navigable. Alice enages is as puzzles — the key fits the door but she is too big; she has to accept the world’s symbolic rules (drink to shrink, eat to grow) to proceed. That shift, from solving the world as expected to reading what it expresses, is exactly the Entrant→Dreamer move the Dreamer role is built on.
Related

Bounded Worlds
The Dreamer
Situated Player Roles

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Annihi.title: Reading - Annihilation (VanderMeer)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Annihi.content:
Novel by Jeff VanderMeer (2014). First book of the Southern Reach trilogy. Amazon
Relevance to Worldbuilding
Four unnamed women enter Area X — a coastal zone sealed off from the world for decades, where nature has reclaimed all human traces. The rules of identity and biology don’t hold inside. A biologist’s husband entered on a previous expedition and returned, but wrong.
Area X is one of the most effective examples of ontological invention in contemporary fiction: the world doesn’t just have different creatures or cultures, it operates under different fundamental rules. The reader never gets a clean explanation. The world resists comprehension by design.
There is also a 2018 film adaptation by Alex Garland — see Film - Annihilation.
Related

Wolf’s Taxonomy of Invention
Nature and Invented Physics
Film - Annihilation

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Dark-E.title: Reading - Dark Eden (Beckett)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Dark-E.content:
Dark Eden is a science fiction novel by Chris Beckett, published in 2012. It won the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 2013.
Summary
The descendants of two stranded astronauts have lived for generations on Eden, a sunless world lit only by bioluminescent trees and geothermal vents. The Family — about 500 people — clings to the original landing site, Circle Valley, waiting for Earth to send a rescue ship. A young man named John Redlantern challenges this stasis, arguing that the Family must spread out and explore beyond the valley. His push to leave splits the community and forces everyone to confront what they’ve built, what they believe, and what they’re willing to lose.
Worldbuilding: Language
One of the novel’s most striking features is its language. The Family’s English has drifted over five generations of isolation. Words repeat for emphasis — “cold cold,” “dark dark” — echoing oral tradition. Profanity and idiom have shifted: “Gela’s tits” (after Angela, the mother of everyone) is a common oath. Concepts that Earth takes for granted have been lost or distorted, preserved only in garbled retellings. “Television” and “lecky-trickity” survive as near-mythic words with no referent.
The effect is a language that sounds like English but sits at a slight angle to it. The reader understands everything but feels the distance — generations of isolation encoded in grammar and vocabulary. It’s worldbuilding through voice rather than exposition.
Worldbuilding: Environment
Eden has no sun. Light comes from the trees themselves — pulsing, humming organisms that blur the line between plant and animal. The world is warm near vents and lethally cold everywhere else. Animals have adapted to the dark: creatures navigate by sound and heat, and the humans have learned to do the same.
The ecosystem is entirely alien but internally consistent. Beckett builds it detail by detail — how people hunt, what they eat, how they navigate, how they mark time without a sun — until Eden feels habitable and specific.
Worldbuilding: Culture and Myth
The Family’s culture is built on retelling. Every generation gathers for “Any Virsries” (anniversaries) to recite the story of Angela and Tommy — the two original castaways. But the story has calcified into ritual. Details are sacred even when misunderstood. The landing site is holy ground. Leaving it is heresy.
This is worldbuilding as cultural anthropology: a society’s myths, taboos, and power structures all trace back to a single origin event, distorted by time and repetition.
Related

Bounded Worlds
Completeness
Cultural Invention

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Emissa.title: Reading - Emissary's Guide to Worlding (Cheng)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Emissa.content:
Author: Ian Cheng · Year: 2018 · Type: Book (short, e-book format)
→ worldto.live · Amazon
Cheng is a visual artist known for AI-driven simulations. This book grew out of his Emissaries trilogy — live simulations shown at MoMA PS1, Serpentine, Carnegie. It formalizes his creative process as a portable framework. His take on worlding functions as advice given to artists broadly, not just to creators who frame their approach as worldbuilding.

“This is not a book about worldbuilding, or how to make your fantasy novel more credible. It’s a book about Worlding. It’s about re-enchanting our complex times by creating futures you can believe in, over and over again.”

The book turns on four ideas, taken up in turn below:

Aliveness and Autonomy — what a World is: the definition, the formula, finite vs. infinite games, Worlding vs. worldbuilding.
The Four Masks — the creative-psychology model: Director, Cartoonist, Hacker, Emissary.
The Container — the medium through which a World first expresses itself.
The Artist’s Dilemma — the tension between control and autonomy in the creative process.


Aliveness and Autonomy
What Is a World?
(pg 17) A World is a future you can believe in: one that promises to survive its creator, and continue generating drama.
An important feature of this definition of a World is its double promise: when a World can “survive its creator,” that means it has achieved sufficient stability to regulate and safeguard its potentiality without authorial intervention. This is a World’s requirement for Autonomy. When a World can “continue generating drama,” a World is sufficiently interesting for people to care about and want to explore. This is a World’s requirement for Aliveness. When a World is keeping its promise, it continues to be a future you can believe in.
What Is Worlding?
(pg 21) Worlding is the artistic activity of an individual artist conceiving, incubating, triggering, and nurturing a World towards aliveness.
Core Definitions
Aliveness — the World generates its own drama; it is self-regulating and self-generating, not solely dependent on the creator’s output.
Autonomy — the World can sustain itself after the creator exits. Cheng distinguishes these: Worlding is firstly the act of creating a life, then secondly letting that life live itself.
The Aliveness Formula
World’s Aliveness = Evidence Usage / Creator’s Hold
Evidence Usage — the sum of all ways the World is used, discussed, extended, believed in. Films watched, forums active, fan fiction written, other creators influenced. When no one uses or believes in the World, Evidence Usage drops to zero.
Creator’s Hold — the degree of authoritative control the creator maintains over what counts as the World. When Creator’s Hold = 1: the World depends entirely on the creator; when the creator exits, the World goes with them. When Creator’s Hold = 0: the World has Autonomy — it can generate new evidence without the creator’s permission.
For example, I throw a party at my home. I provide drinks, board games, music. I choose a time. Perhaps my Creator’s hold is 0.2?
How about 1.0? He references Hayao Miyazaki who strongly authored films such as Spirited Away.
Finite Games and Infinite Games
Cheng draws on philosopher James Carse (Finite and Infinite Games, 1986):

A finite game is played to win — it has defined rules and a defined ending.
An infinite game is played to keep the game going — if it risks ending, the rules must change to sustain it.

The ultimate infinite game, Carse says, is evolutionary life itself: Nature.
A World is the promise of an infinite game. It is “complex enough that we can generatively inhabit it and create new meaning within its local language.”
Worlding vs. Worldbuilding
Cheng explicitly separates these. Worldbuilding constructs a credible, detailed world — geography, history, rules, consistency. Worlding is the process of making a World come alive and sustain itself. The goal of Worlding is Aliveness → Autonomy.

“A World that fails on its promise to ‘survive its creator’ will rot and die soon after its creator exits… A World that fails on its promise to ‘continue generating drama’ becomes a boring utopia populated by the undead.”


The Four Masks
Cheng’s model of the artist as a crew of inner personas — “masks” — each with different drives, strengths, and blind spots. The artist is not one coherent person but a committee fighting to be heard.
Two axes define the masks:

Seeking Home vs. Seeking Surprise — whether the mask drives toward stability and known human values, or toward the frontier and the unknown (experimentation)
Steering by Gut vs. Steering by Story — whether the mask navigates by immediate instinct and feeling, or by long-term arc and context

The masks who Seek Home are rewarded with certainty and security. The masks who Seek Surprise are rewarded with adventure and novelty.
The masks who steer by gut are rewarded with immediate results. The masks who steer by story are rewarded with a sense of big picture context. If the Story cannot expand to incorporate the unexpected, the artist turns to the Gut for survival. And if the Gut proves wrong too many times, the artist looks to Stories to put it all into perspective. It’s judging by short term vs. judging by long term.

The Director
Seeking Home · Steering by Story · Makes “Good” Art
Concerned with recovering meaning from complex problems. Believes that structuring a project correctly creates the conditions for meaningful solutions to emerge. Marshals a team, establishes a narrative throughline, works toward mythology.

Motto: “What’s the story?”
Psychology: Parent seeking home, Adult steering by story
Likes: Longform, mythology, satisfying drama, exploring multiple perspectives, learning from and revising the past, backstory, deep character origins, roadmaps, a good profound cry.
Strengths: Creating the tangible container structure for everyone else to work in. Meaning resonance. Able to narrativize, historicize, mythologize, and organize. Ability to rally a team toward a finite goal that promises to be meaningful.
Weaknesses: Bothered by open-ended outcomes and unsolved mysteries.
Compatible with: Cartoonist, who can help the Director stretch to make instantly recognizable/iconic characters that make the long journey more emotionally resonant, peppered with limbic candy.
Attracted to: Emissary, who can help the Director’s story to expand into sequels, a franchise, a philosophy, or cult following. If only that were manageable and had clear roadmap. Risky with:
Hacker, who could radicalize the project with new abilities for expression, but the Director doesn’t know how to count on it. Threatens to change the Director’s structure, assembled team, budget, and meaning.
Favorite forms: feature film, novel, non-fiction bestsellers, treatise, Oscar nominees
Famous Director-dominant artists: Hayao Miyazaki (animator), Ursula Le Guin (novelist), Jordan Peterson (psychologist), Adam Curtis (filmmaker), Ayn Rand (novelist), Karl Marx (philosopher), Hannah Arendt (philosopher), Margaret Atwood (novelist), Joseph Campbell (mythologist), Homer (epic poet)

The Cartoonist
Seeking Home · Steering by Gut · Makes Flag Art
Concerned with emotional resonance. Reduces complexity into instantly legible signals — characters, symbols, feelings, memes. Plays to the lowest common denominator of human cognition: gut instinct, tribal affiliation, limbic reward.

Mask Archetype: The spontaneous reformer persona who believes we are united by what we feel, and that that baseline human trait is always ripe to be exploited to alleviate immediate pain and uncertainty. The jokester, the politician, the comedian, the marketer, the persuader, the star.
Motto: “FREE PIZZA” Psychology: Parent seeking home, Child steering by gut Likes: Feels, memes, slogans, mnemonics, drama, jokes, irony, attention, animals, bumper stickers, dopamine, serotonin
Strengths: Emotional resonance, characters, archetyping, naming, improv, persuasion
Weaknesses: reducing humanity to their shared inner animal
Compatible with: Director, who can furnish a narrative context, enriching the Cartoonist’s characters and behavioral observations, and add the possibility of character growth.
Attracted to: Hacker, who can offer new magic tricks and psychological models to exploit blind spots in human behavior. Can add wow factor, which adds to limbic resonance.
Risky with: Emissary, who could radicalize the Cartoonist’s work with an ever-growing platform, but the Cartoonist doesn’t know how to count on it. Emissary threatens to demote the Cartoonist’s work to marketing and shame the Cartoonist, whose instincts don’t fit the values of the Emissary’s World.
Favorite forms: social media, elections, talk shows, tabloids, advertising, reality tv, clickbait, news, comedy club
Famous Cartoonist-dominant artists: Oprah Winfrey (talk show host), Andy Warhol (pop artist), Quentin Tarantino (filmmaker), Andy Cohen (reality tv producer), Scott Adams (satirist), Bill Clinton (politician), Kim Kardashian (reality tv personality), Kanye West (recording artist), Mark Twain (satirist)

The Hacker
Seeking Surprise · Steering by Gut · Makes “New” Art
Concerned with disruptive leverage. Sees through the veil of existing worlds to the underlying operating system — the hidden principles and mechanisms. Strips things down to find the real lever, the magic trick, the exploit.

Mask Archetype: The spontaneous disruptor persona who tinkers, breaks and modifies systems, discovers first principles, and unlocks new advantages along the way. The cheat, the con man, the wizard, the magician.
Motto: “It might not be science but it works” Psychology: Adult seeking surprise, Child steering by gut Likes: clever shortcuts, models, first principles, altered states, science fiction
Strengths: Perceives underlying systems. Eye for easy overlooked leverage. Unafraid to break things to find hidden advantage.
Weaknesses: indifferent to context or presentation
Compatible with: Emissary, who can create a sustainable culture around the hack.
Attracted to: Cartoonist. Wants to make their exploit relatable to people, help get a wow factor.
Risky with: Director, could radicalize with narrative meaning, but the Hacker doesn’t know how to count on it. Threatens to turn the hack in service of an ideological purpose.
Favorite forms: apps, cookbooks, playbooks, demos, world’s fair, existing systems, complacent industries
Famous Hacker-dominant artists: Elon Musk (entrepreneur), Nikola Tesla (inventor), Satoshi Nakamoto (blockchain inventor), Dan Barber (chef), Harry Houdini (illusionist)

The Emissary
Seeking Surprise · Steering by Story · Makes Portal Art
Concerned with the long-term health and growth of a living thing. The initiator of Worlding — the one who says let’s create a life, not just a finished object. Thinks on the scale of lifetimes. Absorbs unknowns from Reality and updates the World’s values and systems without losing its core.

“The Emissary is always ‘caught between unravelling old realities and emerging weird ones’ in service of the ongoing health of the World.”

The Emissary is the least practiced mask in art. Its work is thankless: people notice it only when updates don’t serve them, not when the World runs smoothly. The temptation of the Emissary is to hand the World back to the other masks — to let the Director prescribe a final meaning, or the Cartoonist turn it into advertising, or the Hacker sell the superpowers raw.

Motto: “A future you can believe in”
Psychology: Adult seeking surprise, Adult steering by story
Strengths: mission and culture, designing incentives and laws, protecting core values, long-term vision
Weakness: fits everything into the long term; easy to blame for not serving short-term needs
Favorite containers: platforms, series, franchises, think tanks, families
Famous Emissary-dominant figures: Kevin Feige (Marvel), Kathleen Kennedy (Star Wars), Benjamin Franklin, Dalai Lama

Masks Combined
A creation is generally more interesting the more masks it involves. More masks do not result in a more complicated experience for the viewer. On the contrary, if all masks are working together, the viewer feels immersed in a World.





































































CombinationResultC onlya jokeH onlya trickD onlya moralE onlya ruleC + Ha magic actC + Da storyD + Ha playbookC + Ea memeD + Ea wikiH + Ea toolC + D + Ha GesamtkunstwerkC + D + Ea seriesC + H + Ean appD + H + Ea cultC + D + H + Ea World

The Container
Before a World can exist, the artist must choose a container — the medium or form through which the World first expresses itself. A film, a restaurant, a novel, a video game, a religion, an electric car.
The container is not the World. It is a portal to the World.

“A drawing of Mickey Mouse is a low resolution, low dimensional manifestation of the World of Disney. A Mickey cartoon is a bit higher. And Disneyland is a high resolution, high dimensional manifestation of the World of Disney. But even a trip to Disneyland is not a one-to-one experience of the World of Disney itself.”

The Director chooses the container. The Emissary checks whether it implies interesting consequences — whether it has potential for Aliveness.
Declarative vs. Interactive
Containers exist on a spectrum:
Declarative (novel, film, sermon) — the creator declares a world and the audience accepts it. More fantastical potential. Higher suspension of disbelief required. The Cartoonist leads: great characters are needed to make the World sticky.
Interactive (restaurant, app, video game, baby) — the container is inhabited and used. More pragmatically realized. More directly suggests how the World will function. The Hacker leads: a great hack or superpower is needed to make it distinct.

“If you value the pragmatic realization of the eventual World: interactive container > declarative container. If you value the fantastical potential: declarative container > interactive container.”

The Hacker-Led Approach (Interactive Containers)

Discover a hack — test it, confirm it works
Study the hack to understand why it works reliably
See where the hack goes too far; make laws to regulate it
Let the Cartoonist develop characters who embody and violate those laws
Let the Director create a mythological narrative that situates the hack within meaning

The Cartoonist-Led Approach (Declarative Containers)

Devise a character with an inner contradiction
Describe the character by imagining where it lives — the living conditions that created it
The living conditions imply the laws of the World
Imagine disruptors of those laws and the drama that follows

The Container as Contract

“In choosing a container, you are making an explicit contract with the viewer… In return, I will work to surprise your expectations of what is possible by stretching the container a bit farther than you thought it could go.”


The Artist’s Dilemma
Art is not an object, but a special kind of communication between an artist and an audience. It’s a communication for when words won’t do. For when you want to communicate something more interesting, nutritious, complex, or strange. But since high bandwidth telepathy doesn’t exist yet, a mediating object needs to be crafted to articulate this communication: the artwork.
If an artwork is a ship, then the artist is its crew, the content is its cargo, and the destination port is the audience where the communication is received, where the ship docks and the cargo is delivered.

Key Quotes

“A World is conceived when a creator decides to pick some part of Reality and start believing in it again.”


“Simple rules lead to complex behavior. Complicated rules lead to stupid behavior.” — Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, cited by Cheng


“A poem is never finished, only abandoned.” — Paul Valéry, on granting Autonomy

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Kataba.content:
Novella by R.F. Kuang (2024). Amazon
Relevance to Worldbuilding
Katabasis — the descent into the underworld — is one of the oldest worldbuilding moves in storytelling. Kuang’s work engages this mythological structure directly, constructing an underworld with its own logic, rules, and inhabitants. A useful lens for thinking about how worlds built around death and passage function differently from worlds built around habitation.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---On-Exa.title: Reading - On Exactitude in Science (Borges)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---On-Exa.content:
Jorge Luis Borges, Collected Fictions, translated by Andrew Hurley.

…In that Empire, the Art of Cartography attained such Perfection that the map of a single Province occupied the entirety of a City, and the map of the Empire, the entirety of a Province. In time, those Unconscionable Maps no longer satisfied, and the Cartographers Guilds struck a Map of the Empire whose size was that of the Empire, and which coincided point for point with it. The following Generations, who were not so fond of the Study of Cartography as their Forebears had been, saw that that vast Map was Useless, and not without some Pitilessness was it, that they delivered it up to the Inclemencies of Sun and Winters. In the Deserts of the West, still today, there are Tattered Ruins of that Map, inhabited by Animals and Beggars; in all the Land there is no other Relic of the Disciplines of Geography.
—Suarez Miranda, Viajes de varones prudentes, Libro IV, Cap. XLV, Lerida, 1658

A one-paragraph fiction about a map so complete it becomes the territory. The world it describes has achieved total Completeness.
Related

Completeness

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---On-Fai.title: Reading - On Fairy-Stories (Tolkien)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---On-Fai.content:
Author: J.R.R. Tolkien · Year: 1947 · Type: Essay
Tolkien’s argument for why fantasy matters — and what it demands of its maker. The essay introduces his concept of sub-creation, which is the closest thing worldbuilding has to a founding philosophy.

Sub-Creation
Tolkien argues that humans are sub-creators — we make secondary worlds because we are ourselves made. The impulse to build a world isn’t escapism; it’s an expression of something fundamental about being human.

“We make in our measure and in our derivative mode, because we are made: and not only made, but made in the image and likeness of a Maker.”

The primary world (reality) is the raw material. The sub-creator recombines its elements into a secondary world — something new that runs on its own internal logic.
This is exactly the distinction Wolf (p.17) draws when he says fictional worlds exist next to the real world, not inside it.

Secondary Belief
A secondary world succeeds when it induces what Tolkien calls Secondary Belief — the reader’s imaginative absorption. The world has to earn it.
His example: a green sun. You can invent one. But for it to work, the world around it has to be coherent enough that the green sun feels plausible.
This maps directly to Wolf’s concept of plausibility — the world earns belief — and to Consistency and Internal Logic, which is what makes secondary belief possible in the first place.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Pirane.title: Reading - Piranesi (Clarke)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Pirane.content:
Author: Susanna Clarke · Year: 2020 · Type: Novel
→ Amazon
A man known as Piranesi lives in the House: an endless labyrinth of grand halls, their lower floors flooded by tides, their upper halls filled with clouds, every wall lined with statues. He believes the House is the entire world and keeps meticulous journals of its tides and rooms. The novel slowly reveals that the House connects, through hidden ways, to our own world — and how he came to be there.
Relevance to Worldbuilding
Piranesi is a near-perfect Bounded World: the House is a bounded, self-consistent labyrinth the narrator treats as complete in itself, yet it connects to our world through hidden passages. Clarke withholds far more than she explains, making the House a sustained catalyst of speculation — meaning accumulates through the narrator’s patient, committed observation of statues, tides, and halls. It is a vivid case for how a player meets a world.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Situat.title: Reading - Situational Game Design (Upton)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Situat.content:
Author: Brian Upton
Published: 2017 (CRC Press)
A framework for game design centered on the situation — the player’s current state of possibility, constraint, and anticipation. Upton argues that what matters in game design isn’t the formal rules but the felt experience of being in a situation and navigating it forward.
Key idea: a game is a sequence of situations. Good design is the crafting of situations that are legible, interesting, and connected.
Relevance to Worldbuilding
A world is a device for generating situations. The design question shifts from “what are the rules?” to “what situations will the player find themselves in, and do those situations feel meaningful?”
The corpus page Lecture - Situational Game Design for Bounded Worlds works through the first two chapters in detail.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-Fi.title: Reading - The Fifth Season (Jemisin)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-Fi.content:
Novel by N.K. Jemisin (2015). First book of the Broken Earth trilogy. Amazon
Relevance to Worldbuilding
A world built on catastrophe. The Stillness is a single supercontinent wracked by recurring apocalyptic seismic events called Fifth Seasons — civilization-ending disasters that happen often enough that society has organized entirely around surviving them.
Orogenes — people who can sense and manipulate seismic energy — are feared, controlled, and enslaved by the ruling system despite being the only ones who can stop earthquakes. The novel braids three timelines.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-On.title: Reading - The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas (Le Guin)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-On.content:
Author: Ursula K. Le Guin · Year: 1973
A short story set in Omelas, a city of extraordinary happiness and beauty. The story’s central question: the city’s prosperity depends on the suffering of a single child, kept alone in a basement. Everyone knows. Some walk away.
Le Guin calls Omelas a “psychomyth” — a myth about your own ethical imagination.
Relevance to Worldbuilding
Omelas is a world defined entirely by its central dilemma. There is almost no plot, but it provides clear themes of fairness, freedom, and complacency.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-Pl.title: Reading - The Planiverse (Dewdney)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---The-Pl.content:
A.K. Dewdney, The Planiverse: Computer Contact with a Two-Dimensional World (1984)
What It Is
A computer scientist makes contact with a creature named Yendred living in a strictly two-dimensional universe. The book traces what life, physics, biology, architecture, and culture must look like if space has only two dimensions — for example, no passing someone on the street without one of you climbing over the other.
Relevance to Worldbuilding
A clean example of natural invention: one constraint (two spatial dimensions) drives the whole world’s locomotion, doors, digestion, and cities. It also fits ontological invention.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---What-I.title: Reading - What In The World
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---What-I.content:
Authors: von Stackelberg & McDowell (2015)
Source: Journal of Futures Studies

Core Definition

“The process of worldbuilding — the creation of imaginary worlds with coherent geographic, social, cultural, and other features.” (p.32)

This is the foundational academic definition. Zaidi (2019) builds on it, adding that worlds “provide detailed contextual rule sets that develop a larger reality that extends beyond a single story.” See Reading - Worldbuilding in Science Fiction, Foresight and Design (Zaidi).

Four Categories of Speculative Fiction (p.6, citing Levin 2010)
Future-oriented science fiction tends to fall into one of four categories:

Cautionary tales — emphasize consequences (generally negative) of some aspect of today’s society
Thought experiments (“what if” stories) — examine potential impacts of some current or anticipated event, technology, or trend
Literalized metaphors — use a metaphor to study a particular aspect of our world (e.g., space aliens to address alienation from society), making it concrete
Explorations of new science and technology — use new advances as the basis for a storyline

These categories are useful for thinking about which mode a world is operating in — or whether it’s deliberately straddling modes.

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Worldb.filePath: PBOH/Design/_References/Reading - Worldbuilding in Science Fiction, Foresight and Design (Zaidi).md
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Worldb.title: Reading - Worldbuilding in Science Fiction, Foresight and Design (Zaidi)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Worldb.content:
Author: Leah Zaidi (2019)
Source: Journal of Futures Studies

Core Definition (p.17)

“Worldbuilding is the process of constructing a complete and plausible imaginary world that serves as a context for a story. It is ‘the creation of imaginary worlds with coherent geographic, social, cultural, and other features’ (von Stackelberg & McDowell, 2015, p.32). Worlds ‘provide detailed contextual rule sets that develop a larger reality that extends beyond a single story, while potentially providing a deeper understanding of the underlying systems that drive these worlds.‘”


Three Lessons for Worldbuilders (pp.20–21)
1. Designing for Coherence
Ursula K. Le Guin, from Plausibility in Fantasy:

“While I am composing I have no abstract ideas, purposes, or policies in mind, but am intent only on following the story… Then there is detail. The more realistic, exact, ‘factual’ detail in a fantasy story, the more sensually things and acts are imagined and described, the more plausible the world will be. After all, it is a world made entirely of words. Exact and vivid words make an exact and vivid world.”

This connects directly to Consistency and Internal Logic — coherence is built through accumulation of specific, committed detail.
2. User-Testing Worlds
N.K. Jemisin’s process:

“Sometimes I’ll write a short story set in that universe to try and solidify my ideas. Not the same plot, not even the same characters; just playing around with the world. I call this a ‘proof of concept’ story… basically I’m testing the worldbuilding to see if it’s complete enough to support a novel yet. Often the act of writing the story helps me catch glaring holes in my worldbuilding.”

The Fifth Season (2015) — part 1 of the Broken Earth trilogy — is a good starting point for Jemisin.
3. Superstructure of Culture
Gibson and Delaney (via Zaidi): readers of speculative fiction develop a “superstructure of culture” — they build their capacity to engage with alternative systems and ways of living.
Implication: worldbuilding isn’t just entertainment or craft. Engaging with invented worlds trains the imagination to conceive of alternatives. This has potential implications for design, foresight, and social change.

Related

PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Yertle.title: Reading - Yertle the Turtle (Seuss)
PBOH/Design/_References/Reading---Yertle.content:
Author: Dr. Seuss · Year: 1958 · Type: Children’s book
→ Wikipedia · YouTube read-aloud

Summary
Yertle is the king of a small pond. Dissatisfied with his view, he commands the other turtles to stack themselves beneath him so he can sit higher and see — and rule — more. The stack grows taller and taller as Yertle demands ever greater dominion. At the bottom of the stack, a plain little turtle named Mack complains about the pain and hunger the turtles are suffering. Yertle ignores him. Finally, Mack burps — and the whole stack topples. Yertle falls into the mud, and the turtles of the pond are free.

Relevance to Worldbuilding
A fable of power and hierarchy in a bounded world. The pond is the entire world of the story — a Finite world that expands only as Yertle’s ambition piles turtles higher. The world’s edge is felt: Yertle reaches for an outside (the moon), but the system collapses before he arrives. Useful for the Dreamer and Entrant roles — the tyrant’s stack that finally topples is a compact model of a world with stakes built into its structure.
Related

Bounded Worlds
Situated Player Roles

PBOH/Design/_References/World---Backroom.title: World - Backrooms
PBOH/Design/_References/World---Backroom.content:
Origin: 4chan /x/, 2019 | Form: creepypasta → collaborative wiki → found-footage video → feature film
An internet horror phenomenon that grew from a single photograph and one paragraph into a years-long, community-built world. A tiny prompt became a setting, which grew into a multifaceted community worldbuilding project.
The Beginning
It started as one image — a yellow, empty, half-renovated commercial interior — posted to a 4chan thread asking for “disquieting images that just feel ‘off.‘” An anonymous reply named it and gave it a rule:


If you’re not careful and you Noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms, where it’s nothing but the stink of old moist carpet, the madness of mono-yellow, the endless background noise of fluorescent lights at maximum hum-buzz, and the approximately six hundred million square miles of randomly segmented empty rooms to be trapped in.
God save you if you hear something wandering around nearby, because it sure as hell has heard you.

They give an entry rule (noclip — a video-game term for falling through the map when collision fails), an aesthetic (carpet, mono-yellow, fluorescent hum), a scale (six hundred million square miles), and a threat.
The Unseen Thing
This initial image and text demonstrates the withholding that Wolf calls a catalyst of speculation — the gap the audience fills in. In this case, not just in their minds, but the community spent years filling in the world through games, films, and wiki content.
In Bounded Worlds terms the original is a Closed world: an outside (ordinary reality) is implied but withheld — you feel the edge of the maze without ever passing it.
Liminal Space
The Backrooms is the signature example of the liminal space aesthetic: transitional, semi-public built environments — hallways, offices, malls, empty pools, waiting rooms — treated as charged thresholds. Emptied of people and purpose but with their maintenance signs still humming, they produce disorientation and dread. Shira Chess calls this the “institutional gothic”: the haunted castle replaced by fluorescent lights, drop ceilings, and corporate bureaucracy.

The “Poolrooms” (the wiki’s Level 37) — the empty-pool variant of the aesthetic: white tile, warm light, still green water.
A tighter, single-authored take on the same corridor-dread is The Exit 8 — one looping passage with a precise rule.
Creepypasta
The tradition the Backrooms belongs to: short, shareable internet horror stories that spread by copy-paste, reposting, and mutation. They’re folklore native to the web, authorless and endlessly remixed. (Perhaps Slender Man is the most famous earlier example.)
The Wiki Phenomenon
What the community did next demonstrates impressive worldbuilding. Within months the single paragraph became a participatory foundation. The recurring parts:

Levels — the maze became one of many numbered spaces (offices, pools, parking garages).
Entrances and exits — levels connect through “noclip” points and conditions.
Entities — the unseen thing multiplied into a bestiary, each with documented behaviors.
Rules — each level carries survival rules and a danger rating (the wiki’s “Survival Difficulty Class”): how to behave, what to avoid, when you’re safe.
Almond water — a mundane found object (thermoses of liquid) that became the survival resource and informal currency.
The M.E.G. (Major Explorer Group) — a faction of survivors that maps, rescues, and researches. Its real job is to give the wiki an in-world narrator.
Canons — when contributors contradicted each other, the community created parallel canons. Contradiction became a feature, somehting like comic-book multiverses.


Fan-drawn level maps (DeviantArt: Amfstation17, 2022) — the numbered-level taxonomy sketched out by the community, from Level 0: The Lobby onward.
Two wikis carried this — a Fandom wiki (2019, fast and maximalist) and a later Wikidot wiki (2020, more curated and literary).
Invention
All of it is Wolf’s invention at community scale — and all four of his types are present: Nominal (renaming reality the Frontrooms, people wanderers), Cultural (the M.E.G., the almond-water economy, the documentation itself), Natural (entities and level-biomes as invented fauna and landscape), and — the deepest — Ontological (reality has collision seams you can fall through; space is infinite and non-Euclidean).
From Creepypasta to Film
In January 2022, teenage creator Kane Parsons (“Kane Pixels”) released The Backrooms (Found Footage) on YouTube — analog-horror video that re-authored the crowd-sourced premise into a single, filmic continuity (VHS texture, a 1990s research-institute frame). It drew tens of millions of views and studio interest within weeks. That line led to A24’s feature film Backrooms (Parsons directing), released theatrically in 2026.
The Games

Liminal ambience, no monster — POOLS turns the aesthetic into pure navigation dread: no enemies, no UI, no dialogue, just sound, water, and oppressive space.
Atmospheric walking sim — The Complex: Found Footage is a VHS-camera walk through a Backrooms-like world.
Co-op survival horror — Inside the Backrooms has up to four players escape levels by solving puzzles, managing supplies, and learning entity behavior.
Polished multi-level escape — Escape the Backrooms turned the wiki’s level taxonomy into 30+ co-op levels with level-specific exits.


A Roblox rendition — the premise migrated to game platforms and mutated: blue walls instead of mono-yellow, a stray toy chest. A small instance of the parallel canons.
Related

World - The Exit 8 — a single-authored liminal looping world; close kin
Wolf’s Taxonomy of Invention — the kit maps onto all four types of invention
Catalysts of Speculation — the unseen thing; withholding as the engine
Bounded Worlds — the original is a Closed world (an edge felt, never crossed)
Completeness — how much of a world you actually build

PBOH/Design/_References/World---The-Exit.title: World - The Exit 8
PBOH/Design/_References/World---The-Exit.content:
Game: The Exit 8 — Kotake Create, 2023 (PC, Switch) | Film: Exit 8 — dir. Genki Kawamura, 2025
A tiny liminal world: an endless looping underground passageway — a Japanese subway corridor — that you can only escape by reading the space correctly.
The Rule Is the World
The world states its own rules on a sign, and the whole game is obeying them:


Don’t overlook any anomalies.
If you find an anomaly, turn back immediately.
If you don’t find an anomaly, don’t turn back.
Go to Exit 8.


You walk the same corridor again and again. Each loop, something may have changed — a poster, a light, a stain, the man walking toward you. Spot the difference and turn back; if nothing’s wrong, walk on. Get it right and the exit number ticks up — 0, 1, 2 … to Exit 8 and freedom. Get it wrong and you’re back at 0.
This is teaching the rules of the world at its most literal — the world hands you its instructions — and a world built outward from a simple core: attention and memory.
A Looping Closed World
In Bounded Worlds Exit 8 sits at the Closed edge with a Threshold goal: you feel the boundary every loop  until you learn to read the space. Like P.T., the dread comes from a familiar place that should lead somewhere and instead returns you to its own start.
It shares the Backrooms’ liminal-space DNA — fluorescent, anonymous, semi-public architecture emptied of purpose — but where the Backrooms is infinite and authorless, Exit 8 is a single authored loop with a precise rule. Both turn an ordinary transitional space into a trap.
Game → Film
The 2023 game (by studio Kotake Create) became a phenomenon for its purity. In 2025 it became a live-action film — Exit 8, directed by Genki Kawamura, starring Kazunari Ninomiya — which premiered at the Cannes Midnight Screenings (the first live-action video-game adaptation to screen there) and went on to become one of the best-reviewed game-to-film adaptations.
Related

World - Backrooms — the larger liminal-space world this is kin to
Bounded Worlds — a looping Closed world; the edge is felt every loop
Teaching the Rules of the World — the world posts its own instructions

PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.title: Tutorial 1001 - Gemini Terminal Quick Start
PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.content:
0. Introduction
Outcome. By the end of this tutorial, Gemini CLI is installed, pointed at PBOH, and used for your first GET conversation and Prototype Plan.
Use this path only if you prefer a terminal. For the simplest graphical route, use Antigravity Quick Start.
You need: a personal Google account, Node.js 20 or newer, an internet connection, and about 15 minutes.

1. Install Gemini CLI
Open PowerShell on Windows or Terminal on macOS.
Check Node.js:
node -v

If the version is below 20 or the command is missing, install the current LTS release from nodejs.org, then reopen the terminal.
Install and verify Gemini CLI:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini --version


2. Download PBOH

Go to github.com/peterbrinson/PBOH.
Click Code → Download ZIP.
Unzip it, rename PBOH-main to PBOH, and move it to Documents.


3. Launch Gemini in PBOH Folder
In the terminal, change into the folder. One easy method is to type cd , drag the PBOH folder into the terminal, and press Enter.
Then run:
gemini

Sign in with your personal Google account and trust the folder when asked.

4. Start, Talk, and Save
Type:
Start a PBOH session.

Describe a project idea in 4 to 8 sentences and continue until PBOH produces a Prototype Plan. Accept its offer to save the file to student-notes-private/projects/.
If this is a class submission, add Tool: Gemini CLI near the top and save the transcript if your instructor requests it.
Continue with Keep Using PBOH.

Troubleshooting
gemini is not recognized
Close every terminal, open a fresh one, and try gemini --version again.
PowerShell says scripts are disabled
Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser

Close the Administrator window and return to a regular PowerShell window.

PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.title: Tutorial 1005 (Japanese) - Antigravity Quick Start
PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.content:
English version →
0. はじめに
ゴール。 このチュートリアルを終えると、Antigravity で PBOH を開き、プロジェクトのアイデアについて最初の会話を行い、Prototype Plan を自分専用の学生フォルダに保存できます。
必要なもの: 個人の Google アカウント、インターネット接続、約15分。ターミナル、GitHub アカウント、有料プランは必要ありません。

1. PBOH をダウンロードする

github.com/peterbrinson/PBOH を開きます。
緑色の Code ボタンを押し、Download ZIP を選びます。
ZIP を解凍します。

Windows: 右クリック → Extract All…
macOS: ダブルクリック


PBOH-main を PBOH に名前変更し、Documents など見つけやすい場所へ移動します。
フォルダを開き、agent/ と corpus/ が直下にあることを確認します。


2. Antigravity をインストールする

antigravity.google/download から、自分のコンピューター用の Antigravity 2.0 をダウンロードします。
インストールして開きます。
個人の Google アカウントでサインインします。


3. PBOH を開く

Antigravity で新しいプロジェクトを作成します。
フォルダを求められたら、PBOH フォルダそのものを選びます。Documents など親フォルダは選びません。
モデルを選ぶ画面が出たら、現在おすすめされている Pro モデルを使います。


4. PBOH セッションを始める
チャット欄に入力します。
PBOHセッションを始めます。

日本語で会話できます。PBOH は、The Investigator、The Traveler、The Dreamer、または Bounded Worlds のどれに取り組んでいるかを尋ねます。

5. アイデアを伝える
ゲームやプレイ可能な世界のアイデアを4〜8文で説明してください。仕組みだけでなく、プレイヤーにどんな体験をしてほしいかを伝えます。完成したアイデアでなくても構いません。
PBOH が「Here is a Prototype Plan for your project」と言うまで会話を続けます。

6. Prototype Plan を保存する
PBOH が保存を提案したら、承認してください。Antigravity がファイル変更の許可を求めた場合も承認します。保存先は次の場所です。
student-notes-private/projects/prototype-plan-<project-name>.md

授業の提出物にする場合は、ファイルの冒頭に Tool: Gemini (Antigravity) と書きます。先生から求められた場合は、会話全体もコピーまたは書き出してください。
次は Keep Using PBOH に進んでください。

トラブルシューティング
普通のチャットボットのように振る舞う
Antigravity が間違ったフォルダを見ている可能性があります。agent/、corpus/、AGENTS.md を含むフォルダを開き直し、新しいセッションを始めてください。
解凍したフォルダが見つからない
Downloads フォルダを確認してください。Documents に移動し、PBOH に名前変更してから続けます。
サインインできない
学校や職場の管理者によって Gemini が制限されている場合があります。個人の Google アカウントを試してください。

PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.title: Tutorial 1005 - Antigravity Quick Start
PBOH/Development/Tutorials---LLM/Tutoria.content:
0. Introduction
Outcome. By the end of this tutorial, PBOH is open in Antigravity and you have held your first conversation about a project idea. PBOH will save the resulting Prototype Plan in your private student folder.
You need: a personal Google account, an internet connection, and about 15 minutes. You do not need a terminal, GitHub account, or paid plan.

1. Download PBOH

Go to github.com/peterbrinson/PBOH.
Click the green Code button, then Download ZIP.
Unzip the download:

Windows: right-click it → Extract All…
macOS: double-click it


Rename PBOH-main to PBOH and move it somewhere easy to find, such as Documents.
Open the PBOH folder. If it contains only another folder called PBOH-main instead of folders such as agent/ and corpus/, that folder was nested in the ZIP — move that inner folder to Documents instead and rename it PBOH.


2. Install Antigravity

Download Antigravity 2.0 for your computer from antigravity.google/download.
Install and open it.
Sign in with your personal Google account.


3. Open PBOH

In Antigravity, create a new project.
When asked for a folder, choose the PBOH folder itself—not Documents or another parent folder.
If Antigravity asks you to choose a model, use the recommended current Pro model.


4. Start a PBOH Session
Type this in the chat panel:
Start a PBOH session.

You can write in your own language. PBOH will ask whether you are working on The Investigator, The Traveler, The Dreamer, or Bounded Worlds.

5. Bring an Idea
Describe a game or playable-world idea in 4 to 8 sentences. Describe the experience you want the player to have; the idea can still be incomplete.
Continue the conversation until PBOH says, “Here is a Prototype Plan for your project.”

6. Save the Prototype Plan
When PBOH offers to save the Prototype Plan, say yes and approve the file change if Antigravity asks. It should save to:
student-notes-private/projects/prototype-plan-<project-name>.md

If this is a class submission, add Tool: Gemini (Antigravity) near the top. If your instructor asks for the full conversation, also copy or export the transcript.
Continue with Keep Using PBOH.

Troubleshooting
It acts like a normal chatbot
Antigravity is probably looking at the wrong folder. Reopen the folder containing agent/, corpus/, and AGENTS.md, then start a new session.
I cannot find the unzipped folder
Look in Downloads. Move the folder to Documents, rename it PBOH, and continue.
Sign-in does not work
Try a personal Google account rather than a school or workplace account whose administrator may restrict Gemini.

claude

claude is not recognized

Download the app from claude.com/download.
Install and open it.
Sign in with the Claude account that has Claude Code access.
Switch to Code.

Choose the PBOH folder itself—not Documents or another parent folder.
Keep the normal permission setting that asks before changing files.

Start a PBOH session.

Code asks me to upgrade or is missing

Windows mentions Git
Install Git with its default options, fully quit Claude, and reopen it.
